# tp_matrix

Measure what a cross-thread message handoff over the
zc-ring-x1 ring queues actually costs (and where the cost
lives), with four installable binaries: `tp-cell`,
`tp-matrix`, `tp-stream`, and `tp-pool`.

## The measurement, in one paragraph

Both tools run the same experiment, a **cell**: a main thread
sends a counter to a worker over one ring, the worker echoes
it back over a second ring, as fast as the two threads can go
for a fixed duration (one message in flight, so every trip is
a fresh handoff). Every protocol phase is bracketed by two
hardware tick-counter reads and recorded into its own
histogram: the sends (`reserve + fill + commit`, the
producer's cost of placing a message), the recvs (spin wait
for arrival + read + release), and inside each recv the spin
wait itself plus how many polls it took. On Linux the process
also counts its own x-core cache-line fills, cache lines
pulled into a core from another core's cache, via
`perf_event_open` (per-process, worker threads inherited,
user-mode only, no perf(1), root, bash, or scraping), which
is the hardware's answer to "how many cache lines crossed
between the cores per round trip". A cell varies along two
axes: **flavor** (the SPSC v0 ring, the SPSC v1 seam-word
ring, the SPSC v2 in-slot seq ring, and the MPSC v0 and v1
siblings at 1p/1c, every flavor named `xpsc-vN` after its
module path) and **placement** (which CPUs the two threads sit on, same
L3, different L3, SMT siblings, or unpinned).

## tp-matrix: the whole picture, one command

Runs *every* flavor × placement cell (placements discovered
from `/sys` CPU topology) and prints two markdown tables
ready to paste into notes:

- **Phase costs**, per cell: `m.send`, `w.recv`, `w.send`,
  `m.recv` (each `mean/stdev` of the trimmed min-p99 band),
  round trips completed, and `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.
- **Spin decomposition**, the wait inside each recv:
  `spin` (first failed poll -> message visible) and `att`
  (polls per waiting reserve), per side, plus
  `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.

```sh
$ tp-matrix -d 10                  # 20 cells x 10 s on a typical SMT machine, depth 8
$ tp-matrix -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64  # every cell again at each depth
tp-matrix 0.1.0 - run the full measurement matrix, markdown tables out
...
| placement | flavor  | depth |   m.send |     w.recv | ... |  RTs | x-core cache-line fills/RT |
|-----------|---------|------:|---------:|-----------:|-----|-----:|---------------------------:|
| 0,1 CCX   | spsc-v0 |     8 | 22.3/6.0 | 132.5/13.9 | ... | 3.7M |                     10.120 |
| 0,1 CCX   | mpsc-v0 |     8 |  9.5/4.2 |  95.5/19.6 | ... | 5.2M |                      6.617 |
```

`--depth` takes a comma-separated list of ring depths (slots
per ring, powers of two from 1 up), the default `8`, and each
cell repeats per depth. One message is ever in flight, so the
depth changes how many seq words share a line and, at 1,
whether the ring has any slack. The MPSC v0 ring rejects
depth 1, where its protocol wedges (the design note's "MPSC
v1: equality-seq ring"), so its cells there are skipped with a
note naming mpsc-v1, which runs depth 1.

This is the tool that answers "which flavor is faster here,
and why": e.g. on a Zen 2 the SPSC ring moves ~10 cache lines
per round trip to the MPSC ring's ~6.7 and loses cross-core,
but wins on SMT siblings where no lines cross (see
`notes/chores/chores-02.md` for the full analysis).

## tp-stream: the streaming matrix

The round-trip cell keeps one message in flight, so it cannot
say what a ring costs per message when the producer runs ahead
and the ring holds many. `tp-stream` runs the other shape over
the same flavors, placements, and depths: a producer thread
streams a counter as fast as the ring admits for the duration,
a consumer thread drains and checks the order, and the fill
counters divided by the messages moved give the x-core
cache-line fills per message while streaming.

```sh
$ tp-stream -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64
tp-stream 0.1.0 - run the streaming matrix, one markdown table out
...
| placement | flavor  | depth | ns/msg |   msgs | x-core cache-line fills/msg |
|-----------|---------|------:|-------:|-------:|----------------------------:|
| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v1 |    64 |   37.4 | 133.8M |                       0.491 |
| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v2 |    64 |   14.3 | 350.1M |                       0.132 |
```

Two things the streaming number is sensitive to, found while
building the cell and worth knowing before comparing runs:

- The wait policy's inlining: the cell uses the ring crate's
  `policy::spin`, which is `#[inline]`, and an out-of-line
  spin from another crate moved the v2 cross-CCX line from 14
  to 31 ns per message. A poll's cost sets how soon a side
  re-reads a line the other side is writing.
- The producer's loop shape: the cell checks the clock every
  4096 sends, and that check alone moves the v1 cross-CCX line
  from 104 ns per message (1.8 x-core cache-line fills) in a
  plain counted loop to about 40 (0.6). v1 is bistable there: the two sides
  either write its packed seq line in lockstep or the producer
  runs ahead in bursts, and a periodic hiccup on the producer
  tips it into the second. v0 and v2 read the same in both
  loop shapes. The demo's stream lines are the plain loop.

## tp-pool: the pool-message sweep

The two matrices above write the payload into the ring's slot.
The messaging layer's loop is the other shape: take a message
from the pool, fill it, push its reference, receive it,
process it, return it to the pool. `tp-pool` runs that loop a
fixed count of messages per cell over the descriptor rings,
`spsc-v2` and `mpsc-v1` carrying a `Desc`, and over cordyceps's
`MpscQueue`, Vyukov's intrusive MPSC, linked through the same
pool's buffers, so the queue is the only variable between the
rows. The pool bounds the messages in flight, so its size is
the axis every flavor shares, the columns. A ring depth at or
above the pool size never reports Full, so that row is the
ring at the pool's bound and the rows below it are the ring
throttling first, and the cordyceps row, unbounded, has no
depth.

```sh
$ tp-pool                                  # pools 1,100,1000; depths 1,8,64,1024; 1M messages; median of 3
$ tp-pool --pool 1,10,100 --depth 1,1024 --count 200000 --repeat 5
tp-pool 0.1.0 - run the pool-message sweep, one table per placement
...
0,3 x-CCX: ns/msg

| flavor    | depth | pool=1 | pool=100 | pool=1000 |
|-----------|-------|-------:|---------:|----------:|
| spsc-v2   | 1024  |  504.2 |    214.9 |     215.0 |
| cordyceps | -     |  615.0 |    213.7 |     217.2 |
```

Each placement gets an `ns/msg` table and an
`x-core cache-line fills/msg` table of the same shape. The cordyceps consumer waits on
`Inconsistent`, a producer between its head swap and its link
store, as it waits on `Empty`, so that window's cost is in the
row's ns/msg as a ring consumer's polls are in its. The pool's
free-stack is in every row: the consumer's free pushes the
buffer it just read, and the producer's alloc pops that same
buffer, so a line the consumer wrote crosses back on every
message whatever the queue does, which is why these numbers sit
far above the in-slot tables' at the same placement.

## tp-cell: one cell, under the microscope

Runs a single placement (your `--pin` choice, or unpinned)
and prints the *full* per-probe percentile band tables that
the matrix summarizes to `mean/stdev` (min/p1/.../p99/max
rows with first/last/range/count/mean columns), plus the raw
fill counters:

```sh
$ tp-cell spsc-v0 -d 5 --pin 0,1
tp-cell 0.1.0 - run one phase-probed ring round-trip cell
spsc-v0 round trip [duration=5.0s pin=main=0,worker=1]:
  tprobe: spsc-v0 main send (reserve+commit) [count=21,078,016]
    ...band rows...
  ...seven more probes, trip order...
  fill counters: lcl_cache=209,239,903 (9.927 x-core cache-line fills/RT)  lcl_l2=249,403  ...
```

Use it when a matrix row looks odd and you want the shape of
the distribution (bimodality, tail weight), or to A/B one
placement while changing something.

## Build / test / install

```sh
cargo build -p tp_matrix
cargo test --workspace
cargo install --path tp_matrix --locked   # installs tp-cell, tp-matrix, tp-stream, tp-pool
```

`--locked` builds from the committed `Cargo.lock`, so a saved
run's banner names a build another machine can reproduce.

`-h` for a summary of the flags, `--help` for details. Both
print the `name version - tagline` banner first, as does
every run (so saved output identifies the build it came
from).

## Requirements and caveats

- Fill counters need `kernel.perf_event_paranoid ≤ 2` (the
  usual default, self-profiling only). Without them the
  tools still run, and the fill columns read `-`.
- The fill events are AMD Zen 2 raw encodings, A/B-verified
  against `perf stat`. Other microarchitectures need their
  own encodings in `tp_runner::perf`.
- Non-Linux builds run unpinned without counters.
- The crates: probes are `tprobe`, generic runner machinery
  (CLI, pinning, drive loop, perf, topology) is `tp_runner`.
  This crate holds only the ring-aware cells and the four
  binaries.

content.content:
15	hardware tick-counter reads and recorded into its own
16	histogram: the sends (`reserve + fill + commit`, the
17	producer's cost of placing a message), the recvs (spin wait
18	for arrival + read + release), and inside each recv the spin
19	wait itself plus how many polls it took. On Linux the process
20	also counts its own x-core cache-line fills, cache lines
21	pulled into a core from another core's cache, via
22	`perf_event_open` (per-process, worker threads inherited,
23	user-mode only, no perf(1), root, bash, or scraping), which
24	is the hardware's answer to "how many cache lines crossed
25	between the cores per round trip". A cell varies along two
26	axes: **flavor** (the SPSC v0 ring, the SPSC v1 seam-word
27	ring, the SPSC v2 in-slot seq ring, and the MPSC v0 and v1
28	siblings at 1p/1c, every flavor named `xpsc-vN` after its
29	module path) and **placement** (which CPUs the two threads sit on, same
30	L3, different L3, SMT siblings, or unpinned).
31	
32	## tp-matrix: the whole picture, one command
33	
34	Runs *every* flavor × placement cell (placements discovered
35	from `/sys` CPU topology) and prints two markdown tables
36	ready to paste into notes:
37	
38	- **Phase costs**, per cell: `m.send`, `w.recv`, `w.send`,
39	  `m.recv` (each `mean/stdev` of the trimmed min-p99 band),
40	  round trips completed, and `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.
41	- **Spin decomposition**, the wait inside each recv:
42	  `spin` (first failed poll -> message visible) and `att`
43	  (polls per waiting reserve), per side, plus
44	  `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.
45	
46	```sh
47	$ tp-matrix -d 10                  # 20 cells x 10 s on a typical SMT machine, depth 8
48	$ tp-matrix -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64  # every cell again at each depth
49	tp-matrix 0.1.0 - run the full measurement matrix, markdown tables out
50	...
51	| placement | flavor  | depth |   m.send |     w.recv | ... |  RTs | x-core cache-line fills/RT |
52	|-----------|---------|------:|---------:|-----------:|-----|-----:|---------------------------:|
53	| 0,1 CCX   | spsc-v0 |     8 | 22.3/6.0 | 132.5/13.9 | ... | 3.7M |                     10.120 |
54	| 0,1 CCX   | mpsc-v0 |     8 |  9.5/4.2 |  95.5/19.6 | ... | 5.2M |                      6.617 |
55	```
56	
57	`--depth` takes a comma-separated list of ring depths (slots
58	per ring, powers of two from 1 up), the default `8`, and each
59	cell repeats per depth. One message is ever in flight, so the
60	depth changes how many seq words share a line and, at 1,
61	whether the ring has any slack. The MPSC v0 ring rejects
62	depth 1, where its protocol wedges (the design note's "MPSC
63	v1: equality-seq ring"), so its cells there are skipped with a
64	note naming mpsc-v1, which runs depth 1.
65	
66	This is the tool that answers "which flavor is faster here,
67	and why": e.g. on a Zen 2 the SPSC ring moves ~10 cache lines
68	per round trip to the MPSC ring's ~6.7 and loses cross-core,
69	but wins on SMT siblings where no lines cross (see
70	`notes/chores/chores-02.md` for the full analysis).
71	
72	## tp-stream: the streaming matrix
73	
74	The round-trip cell keeps one message in flight, so it cannot
75	say what a ring costs per message when the producer runs ahead
76	and the ring holds many. `tp-stream` runs the other shape over
77	the same flavors, placements, and depths: a producer thread
78	streams a counter as fast as the ring admits for the duration,
79	a consumer thread drains and checks the order, and the fill
80	counters divided by the messages moved give the x-core
81	cache-line fills per message while streaming.
82	
83	```sh
84	$ tp-stream -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64
85	tp-stream 0.1.0 - run the streaming matrix, one markdown table out
86	...
87	| placement | flavor  | depth | ns/msg |   msgs | x-core cache-line fills/msg |
88	|-----------|---------|------:|-------:|-------:|----------------------------:|
89	| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v1 |    64 |   37.4 | 133.8M |                       0.491 |
90	| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v2 |    64 |   14.3 | 350.1M |                       0.132 |
91	```
92	
93	Two things the streaming number is sensitive to, found while
94	building the cell and worth knowing before comparing runs:
95	
96	- The wait policy's inlining: the cell uses the ring crate's
97	  `policy::spin`, which is `#[inline]`, and an out-of-line
98	  spin from another crate moved the v2 cross-CCX line from 14
99	  to 31 ns per message. A poll's cost sets how soon a side
100	  re-reads a line the other side is writing.
101	- The producer's loop shape: the cell checks the clock every
102	  4096 sends, and that check alone moves the v1 cross-CCX line
103	  from 104 ns per message (1.8 x-core cache-line fills) in a
104	  plain counted loop to about 40 (0.6). v1 is bistable there: the two sides
105	  either write its packed seq line in lockstep or the producer
106	  runs ahead in bursts, and a periodic hiccup on the producer
107	  tips it into the second. v0 and v2 read the same in both
108	  loop shapes. The demo's stream lines are the plain loop.
109	
110	## tp-pool: the pool-message sweep
111	
112	The two matrices above write the payload into the ring's slot.
113	The messaging layer's loop is the other shape: take a message
114	from the pool, fill it, push its reference, receive it,
115	process it, return it to the pool. `tp-pool` runs that loop a

file.content:
hardware tick-counter reads and recorded into its own
histogram: the sends (`reserve + fill + commit`, the
producer's cost of placing a message), the recvs (spin wait
for arrival + read + release), and inside each recv the spin
wait itself plus how many polls it took. On Linux the process
also counts its own x-core cache-line fills, cache lines
pulled into a core from another core's cache, via
`perf_event_open` (per-process, worker threads inherited,
user-mode only, no perf(1), root, bash, or scraping), which
is the hardware's answer to "how many cache lines crossed
between the cores per round trip". A cell varies along two
axes: **flavor** (the SPSC v0 ring, the SPSC v1 seam-word
ring, the SPSC v2 in-slot seq ring, and the MPSC v0 and v1
siblings at 1p/1c, every flavor named `xpsc-vN` after its
module path) and **placement** (which CPUs the two threads sit on, same
L3, different L3, SMT siblings, or unpinned).

## tp-matrix: the whole picture, one command

Runs *every* flavor × placement cell (placements discovered
from `/sys` CPU topology) and prints two markdown tables
ready to paste into notes:

- **Phase costs**, per cell: `m.send`, `w.recv`, `w.send`,
  `m.recv` (each `mean/stdev` of the trimmed min-p99 band),
  round trips completed, and `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.
- **Spin decomposition**, the wait inside each recv:
  `spin` (first failed poll -> message visible) and `att`
  (polls per waiting reserve), per side, plus
  `x-core cache-line fills/RT`.

```sh
$ tp-matrix -d 10                  # 20 cells x 10 s on a typical SMT machine, depth 8
$ tp-matrix -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64  # every cell again at each depth
tp-matrix 0.1.0 - run the full measurement matrix, markdown tables out
...
| placement | flavor  | depth |   m.send |     w.recv | ... |  RTs | x-core cache-line fills/RT |
|-----------|---------|------:|---------:|-----------:|-----|-----:|---------------------------:|
| 0,1 CCX   | spsc-v0 |     8 | 22.3/6.0 | 132.5/13.9 | ... | 3.7M |                     10.120 |
| 0,1 CCX   | mpsc-v0 |     8 |  9.5/4.2 |  95.5/19.6 | ... | 5.2M |                      6.617 |
```

`--depth` takes a comma-separated list of ring depths (slots
per ring, powers of two from 1 up), the default `8`, and each
cell repeats per depth. One message is ever in flight, so the
depth changes how many seq words share a line and, at 1,
whether the ring has any slack. The MPSC v0 ring rejects
depth 1, where its protocol wedges (the design note's "MPSC
v1: equality-seq ring"), so its cells there are skipped with a
note naming mpsc-v1, which runs depth 1.

This is the tool that answers "which flavor is faster here,
and why": e.g. on a Zen 2 the SPSC ring moves ~10 cache lines
per round trip to the MPSC ring's ~6.7 and loses cross-core,
but wins on SMT siblings where no lines cross (see
`notes/chores/chores-02.md` for the full analysis).

## tp-stream: the streaming matrix

The round-trip cell keeps one message in flight, so it cannot
say what a ring costs per message when the producer runs ahead
and the ring holds many. `tp-stream` runs the other shape over
the same flavors, placements, and depths: a producer thread
streams a counter as fast as the ring admits for the duration,
a consumer thread drains and checks the order, and the fill
counters divided by the messages moved give the x-core
cache-line fills per message while streaming.

```sh
$ tp-stream -d 5 --depth 1,2,8,64
tp-stream 0.1.0 - run the streaming matrix, one markdown table out
...
| placement | flavor  | depth | ns/msg |   msgs | x-core cache-line fills/msg |
|-----------|---------|------:|-------:|-------:|----------------------------:|
| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v1 |    64 |   37.4 | 133.8M |                       0.491 |
| 0,3 x-CCX | spsc-v2 |    64 |   14.3 | 350.1M |                       0.132 |
```

Two things the streaming number is sensitive to, found while
building the cell and worth knowing before comparing runs:

- The wait policy's inlining: the cell uses the ring crate's
  `policy::spin`, which is `#[inline]`, and an out-of-line
  spin from another crate moved the v2 cross-CCX line from 14
  to 31 ns per message. A poll's cost sets how soon a side
  re-reads a line the other side is writing.
- The producer's loop shape: the cell checks the clock every
  4096 sends, and that check alone moves the v1 cross-CCX line
  from 104 ns per message (1.8 x-core cache-line fills) in a
  plain counted loop to about 40 (0.6). v1 is bistable there: the two sides
  either write its packed seq line in lockstep or the producer
  runs ahead in bursts, and a periodic hiccup on the producer
  tips it into the second. v0 and v2 read the same in both
  loop shapes. The demo's stream lines are the plain loop.

## tp-pool: the pool-message sweep

The two matrices above write the payload into the ring's slot.
The messaging layer's loop is the other shape: take a message
from the pool, fill it, push its reference, receive it,
process it, return it to the pool. `tp-pool` runs that loop a
fixed count of messages per cell over the descriptor rings,
`spsc-v2` and `mpsc-v1` carrying a `Desc`, and over cordyceps's
`MpscQueue`, Vyukov's intrusive MPSC, linked through the same
pool's buffers, so the queue is the only variable between the
rows. The pool bounds the messages in flight, so its size is
the axis every flavor shares, the columns. A ring depth at or
above the pool size never reports Full, so that row is the
ring at the pool's bound and the rows below it are the ring
throttling first, and the cordyceps row, unbounded, has no
depth.

```sh
$ tp-pool                                  # pools 1,100,1000; depths 1,8,64,1024; 1M messages; median of 3
$ tp-pool --pool 1,10,100 --depth 1,1024 --count 200000 --repeat 5
tp-pool 0.1.0 - run the pool-message sweep, one table per placement
...
0,3 x-CCX: ns/msg

| flavor    | depth | pool=1 | pool=100 | pool=1000 |
|-----------|-------|-------:|---------:|----------:|
| spsc-v2   | 1024  |  504.2 |    214.9 |     215.0 |
| cordyceps | -     |  615.0 |    213.7 |     217.2 |
```

Each placement gets an `ns/msg` table and an
`x-core cache-line fills/msg` table of the same shape. The cordyceps consumer waits on
`Inconsistent`, a producer between its head swap and its link
store, as it waits on `Empty`, so that window's cost is in the
row's ns/msg as a ring consumer's polls are in its. The pool's
free-stack is in every row: the consumer's free pushes the
buffer it just read, and the producer's alloc pops that same
buffer, so a line the consumer wrote crosses back on every
message whatever the queue does, which is why these numbers sit
far above the in-slot tables' at the same placement.

## tp-cell: one cell, under the microscope

Runs a single placement (your `--pin` choice, or unpinned)
and prints the *full* per-probe percentile band tables that
the matrix summarizes to `mean/stdev` (min/p1/.../p99/max
rows with first/last/range/count/mean columns), plus the raw
fill counters:

```sh
$ tp-cell spsc-v0 -d 5 --pin 0,1
tp-cell 0.1.0 - run one phase-probed ring round-trip cell
spsc-v0 round trip [duration=5.0s pin=main=0,worker=1]:
  tprobe: spsc-v0 main send (reserve+commit) [count=21,078,016]
    ...band rows...
  ...seven more probes, trip order...
  fill counters: lcl_cache=209,239,903 (9.927 x-core cache-line fills/RT)  lcl_l2=249,403  ...
```

Use it when a matrix row looks odd and you want the shape of
the distribution (bimodality, tail weight), or to A/B one
placement while changing something.

## Build / test / install

```sh
cargo build -p tp_matrix
cargo test --workspace
cargo install --path tp_matrix --locked   # installs tp-cell, tp-matrix, tp-stream, tp-pool
```

`--locked` builds from the committed `Cargo.lock`, so a saved
run's banner names a build another machine can reproduce.

`-h` for a summary of the flags, `--help` for details. Both
print the `name version - tagline` banner first, as does
every run (so saved output identifies the build it came
from).

## Requirements and caveats

- Fill counters need `kernel.perf_event_paranoid ≤ 2` (the
  usual default, self-profiling only). Without them the
  tools still run, the fill columns read `-`, and `tp-cell`'s
  fill counters line reads unavailable.

- `placement`: the CPUs main and the worker are pinned to, and how they share caches: CCX same L3, x-CCX different L3, SMT one core's two threads, or unpinned
- `flavor`: the ring both directions run over
- `depth`: slots per ring. One message is in flight, so depth changes which words share a cache line and, at 1, whether the ring has slack
- `m.send`: main's send, reserve + fill + commit, ns as mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band
- `w.recv`: worker's recv, spin wait + read + release, ns as mean/stdev
- `w.spin`: the wait inside w.recv, first failed poll to reserve success, ns as mean/stdev, waiting reserves only
- `w.att`: polls per waiting reserve inside w.recv, as mean/stdev
- `w.send`: worker's send, reserve + fill + commit, ns as mean/stdev
- `m.recv`: main's recv, spin wait + read + release, ns as mean/stdev
- `m.spin`: the wait inside m.recv, ns as mean/stdev, waiting reserves only
- `m.att`: polls per waiting reserve inside m.recv, as mean/stdev
- `RTs`: round trips completed in the cell's duration, in millions
- `xfills/RT`: x-core cache-line fills, cache lines pulled into a core from another core's cache (0 when the threads share a core's caches, as SMT siblings do), per round trip

content.content:
- `placement`: the CPUs the two threads are pinned to and how they share caches:
  CCX two cores on one L3, x-CCX cores on different L3s, SMT one core's two
  hardware threads sharing its L1 and L2, or unpinned
- `flavor`: the ring both directions of the round trip run over
- `depth`: slots per ring. One message is ever in flight, so depth changes which
  seq words share a cache line and, at 1, whether the ring has any slack
- `m.send`: main's send, reserve + fill + commit, the producer's cost of placing
  a message, ns as mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band
- `w.recv`: the worker's recv, spin wait for arrival + read + release, ns as
  mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band
- `w.spin`: the wait inside w.recv, first failed poll to reserve success, ns as
  mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band, recorded only for reserves that waited
- `w.att`: polls per waiting reserve inside w.recv, as mean/stdev of the trimmed
  min-p99 band
- `w.send`: the worker's send, reserve + fill + commit, the producer's cost of
  placing a message, ns as mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band
- `m.recv`: main's recv, spin wait for arrival + read + release, ns as
  mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band
- `m.spin`: the wait inside m.recv, first failed poll to reserve success, ns as
  mean/stdev of the trimmed min-p99 band, recorded only for reserves that waited
- `m.att`: polls per waiting reserve inside m.recv, as mean/stdev of the trimmed
  min-p99 band
- `RTs`: round trips completed in the cell's duration, in millions
- `xfills/RT`: x-core cache-line fills: cache lines pulled into a core from
  another core's cache, near 0 when the threads share a core's caches, as SMT
  siblings do, per round trip
===
| flavor    | depth | pool=1 | pool=100 | pool=1000 |
|-----------|-------|-------:|---------:|----------:|
| spsc-v2   | 1     |  7.202 |    7.509 |     7.514 |
| mpsc-v1   | 1     | 10.211 |    9.918 |    10.050 |
| cordyceps | -     |  9.040 |    4.234 |     0.477 |

- `placement`: the CPUs the two threads are pinned to and
  how they share caches: CCX two cores on one L3, x-CCX
  cores on different L3s, SMT one core's two hardware
  threads sharing its L1 and L2, or unpinned
- `ns/msg`: elapsed ns over messages for each cell, the
  median of the runs by elapsed time
- `xfills/msg`: x-core cache-line fills: cache lines pulled
  into a core from another core's cache, near 0 when the
  threads share a core's caches, as SMT siblings do, per
  message, from the same median run
- `flavor`: the queue the pool's messages cross: a
  descriptor ring carrying a Desc, or cordyceps's intrusive
  queue linked through the pool's own buffers
- `depth`: slots in the ring, `-` for cordyceps, which is
  unbounded. A depth at or above the pool size never reports
  Full
- `pool=N`: the pool's buffer count, the bound on messages
  in flight
===

from `/sys` CPU topology) and prints one markdown table ready

- `placement`: the CPUs the two threads are pinned to and
  how they share caches: CCX two cores on one L3, x-CCX
  cores on different L3s, SMT one core's two hardware

  median of the runs by elapsed time

  into a core from another core's cache, near 0 when the
  threads share a core's caches, as SMT siblings do, per
  message, from the same median run
- `flavor`: the queue the pool's messages cross: a
  descriptor ring carrying a Desc, or cordyceps's intrusive
  queue linked through the pool's own buffers
- `depth`: slots in the ring, `-` for cordyceps, which is
  unbounded. A depth at or above the pool size never reports
  Full
- `pool=N`: the pool's buffer count, the bound on messages
  in flight

- `<placement>`: the prefix of each table title, the CPUs

  CCX two cores on one L3, x-CCX cores on different L3s, SMT
  one core's two hardware threads sharing its L1 and L2, or
  unpinned
- `<placement>: ns/msg`: a table whose cells are elapsed ns
  over messages at the row's flavor and depth and the
  column's pool size, the median of the runs by elapsed time
- `<placement>: xfills/msg`: a table of the same cells'

  from another core's cache, near 0 when the threads share a
  core's caches, as SMT siblings do, per message, from the
  same median run

  queue linked through the pool's own buffers

  Full

##### refactor: xfills label and one tp-matrix table

The tools' fill columns were labeled by the perf event, so a reader had to know the event to read
the number, their meanings lived in one banner line past a terminal's width, `tp-matrix` split one
row of measurements across two tables, and the mpsc-v0 skip named a floor without saying what it
was or what runs below it.

* The label named the counter, not the reading.
  - The columns read `xfills`, spelled out once for the four tools by `XFILLS_MEANING`, and the
    README defines it as cache lines pulled into a core from another core's cache. Code identifiers
    keep the event's vocabulary.
* Column meanings were packed into the banner, and some columns had none.
  - `-v` prints a markdown list under each table, one item per column, wrapped to the table's width
    within 60 to 80 columns, and the line under the banner names `-v`, so a default run stays the
    tables alone and a pasted table can carry its key.
* `tp-matrix`'s spin table repeated its phase table's key columns.

1	//! The pool-message sweep cells: the messaging layer's loop,
2	//! take a message from the pool, fill it, push its reference,
3	//! receive it, process it, return it, run over the descriptor
4	//! rings and cordyceps's intrusive queue on one pool, so the
5	//! queue is the only variable between rows.
6	//!
7	//! - The pool bounds the traffic: with `pool_size` buffers at
8	//!   most that many messages are in flight, so a ring depth at
9	//!   or above it never reports Full, and the cordyceps row,
10	//!   whose queue is unbounded, has no depth at all.
11	//! - Every row allocs from and frees to the same pool: the
12	//!   rings carry a `Desc`, cordyceps carries the buffer's
13	//!   pointer with the queue's link inside the buffer, and its
14	//!   consumer maps the pointer back to the buffer's index for
15	//!   the free.
16	//! - A cell moves a fixed count of messages, so its number is
17	//!   elapsed over count, the thread spawn inside it alike for
18	//!   every row, and the fill counters over the whole cell give
19	//!   the lines crossed per message.
20	
21	use std::ptr::{self, NonNull};
22	use std::time::Instant;
23	
24	use cordyceps::Linked;
25	use cordyceps::mpsc_queue::{Links, MpscQueue, TryDequeueError};
26	use tp_runner::{LineBuf, pin_to_cpu, unpin_current};
27	use zc_ring_x1::{CACHE_LINE_SIZE, Desc, Pool, PoolHeader, PoolRegistry, policy};
28	use zerocopy::{FromBytes, Immutable, IntoBytes, KnownLayout};
29	
30	use crate::FillCounts;

content.content:
The two matrices above write the payload into the ring's slot.
The messaging layer's loop is the other shape: take a message
from the pool, fill it, push its reference, receive it,
process it, return it to the pool. `tp-pool` runs that loop a
fixed count of messages per cell over the descriptor rings,
`spsc-v2` and `mpsc-v1` carrying a `Desc`, and over cordyceps's
`MpscQueue`, Vyukov's intrusive MPSC, linked through the same
pool's buffers, so the queue is the only variable between the
rows. The pool bounds the messages in flight, so its size is
the axis every flavor shares, the columns. A ring depth at or
above the pool size never reports Full, so that row is the
ring at the pool's bound and the rows below it are the ring
throttling first, and the cordyceps row, unbounded, has no
depth.

```sh
$ tp-pool                                  # pools 1,100,1000; depths 1,8,64,1024; 1M messages; median of 3
$ tp-pool --pool 1,10,100 --depth 1,1024 --count 200000 --repeat 5
tp-pool 0.1.0 - run the pool-message sweep, one table per placement
...
0,3 x-CCX: ns/msg

The duration rung is ready for review. Full validation passed, clippy on `tp_matrix` is clean, and the tools are reinstalled.

**How a pool cell runs now (`pool.rs`)**
- **Producer:** it checks the clock every `STREAM_CHECK_EVERY` (4096) messages, the same way `tp-stream`'s producer does. Once the duration has passed, it sends one more pool message with `seq = STOP`.
- **Consumer:** it keeps receiving, asserting order, and freeing. When it sees `STOP`, it frees that message and returns how many it received, so the pool is back to full at the end of every cell.
- **Scope:** this covers all three cells, `spsc-v2`, `mpsc-v1`, and cordyceps.
- **Results:** `PoolResult` now carries `msgs`.
- **Helper:** `STREAM_CHECK_EVERY` is now `pub(crate)` so `pool.rs` can reuse it.

**`tp-pool` itself**
- `--count` is gone, and passing it is now an error.
- `-d/--duration <SECS>` replaces it, default 0.1. Zero, negative, and non-numbers are rejected.
- ns/msg and xfills/msg now divide by the messages actually moved.
- The median run is chosen by ns per message.
- The banner reads `60 cells, 0.1s each, median of 3 runs`, and a custom value prints as given, e.g. `0.02s`.

**Check against the old runs.** A default-duration run at 0,1 CCX gave numbers in line with the count-based runs: spsc-v2 at depth 1 was 144.9, 108.7, and 109.2 ns/msg across the three pool sizes. That sweep of 60 cells, three runs each, took about 9 seconds.

# tp_matrix

Measure what a cross-thread message handoff over the
zc-ring-x1 ring queues actually costs (and where the cost
lives), with four installable binaries: `tp-cell`,

it back over a second ring, as fast as the two threads can go

## The measurement, in one paragraph

`tp-cell` and `tp-matrix` run the same experiment, a **cell**: a main thread
sends a counter to a worker over one ring, the worker echoes
it back over a second ring, as fast as the two threads can go
for a fixed duration (one message in flight, so every trip is
a fresh handoff). Every protocol phase is bracketed by two
hardware tick-counter reads and recorded into its own
histogram: the sends (`reserve + fill + commit`, the
producer's cost of placing a message), the recvs (spin wait
for arrival + read + release), and inside each recv the spin
wait itself plus how many polls it took. On Linux the process
also counts its own x-core cache-line fills (`xfills` in the
tables), cache lines pulled into a core from another core's
cache, via
`perf_event_open` (per-process, worker threads inherited,
user-mode only, no perf(1), root, bash, or scraping), which
is the hardware's answer to "how many cache lines crossed
between the cores per round trip". A cell varies along two
axes: **flavor** (the SPSC v0 ring, the SPSC v1 seam-word
ring, the SPSC v2 in-slot seq ring, and the MPSC v0 and v1
siblings at 1p/1c, every flavor named `xpsc-vN` after its
module path) and **placement** (which CPUs the two threads sit on, same
L3, different L3, SMT siblings, or unpinned).

| Payload | counter in the slot | counter in the slot | counter in the slot | pool buffer, its `Desc` or pointer crosses |
| Depth | seq sharing, slack at 1 | seq sharing, slack at 1 | how far the producer can run ahead | throttles when below the pool size |
| Runs | `-d` per cell | `-d` per cell | `-d` per cell | `-d` per run, median of `--repeat` |
| Reports | full percentile bands per phase | mean/stdev per phase, RTs, xfills/RT | ns/msg, msgs, xfills/msg | ns/msg and xfills/msg per pool size |
| Flavors | the five rings | the five rings | the five rings | spsc-v2, mpsc-v1, cordyceps |

## tp-cell: one cell, under the microscope

Runs a single placement (your `--pin` choice, or unpinned)
and prints the *full* per-probe percentile band tables that
the matrix summarizes to `mean/stdev` (min/p1/.../p99/max
rows with first/last/range/count/mean columns), plus the raw
fill counters:

```sh
$ tp-cell spsc-v0 -d 5 --pin 0,1 -v
tp-cell 0.1.0 - run one phase-probed ring round-trip cell
spsc-v0 round trip [duration=5.0s pin=main=0,worker=1]:
  tprobe: spsc-v0 main send (reserve+commit) [count=21,078,016]
    ...band rows...
  ...seven more probes, trip order...
  fill counters: lcl_cache=209,239,903 (9.927 xfills/RT)  lcl_l2=249,403  ...

- `lcl_cache`: demand fills served from another core's cache
...
```

Use it when a matrix row looks odd and you want the shape of
the distribution (bimodality, tail weight), or to A/B one
placement while changing something.

## tp-matrix: the whole picture, one command

Runs *every* flavor × placement cell (placements discovered
from `/sys` CPU topology) and prints one markdown table ready
to paste into notes, a row per cell with its columns in trip
order: `m.send`, then `w.recv` with the `w.spin` and `w.att`
store, as it waits on `Empty`, so that window's cost is in the
row's ns/msg as a ring consumer's polls are in its. The pool's
free-stack is in every row: the consumer's free pushes the
buffer it just read, and the producer's alloc pops that same
buffer, so a line the consumer wrote crosses back on every
message whatever the queue does, which is why these numbers sit
far above the in-slot tables' at the same placement.

### Against `tp-matrix --depth 1,8,64,1024`

Both have a depth axis, and the depth means different things.

- `tp-matrix` keeps one message in flight, so depth never
  throttles. It only changes which seq words share a cache
  line, and at 1 whether the ring has slack. A row is a round
  trip, two handoffs.
- `tp-pool` lets up to the pool size run ahead, so a depth
  below the pool size throttles the producer. A row is one
  handoff plus a pool alloc and free.
- The closest match is `tp-pool` at pool=1 against `tp-matrix`
  at depth 1, halved for the two handoffs. `tp-pool` still pays
  for the pool's free-stack line crossing back on every
  message, so it reads higher.

## Reading xfills at an SMT pair

xfills counts cache lines a core pulls from another core's
cache. SMT siblings are one core's two threads sharing its L1
and L2, so nothing crosses and xfills reads near 0, about
0.0005 per message, background noise. That is expected, not a
fault.

## What belongs in iiac-perf

- `tp-pool` goes: its loop is the messaging layer's shape,
  and iiac-perf takes it and the design note's `Measured:
  pool-message sweep` as its model.
- `tp-stream` is a candidate: streaming throughput is a
  generic benchmark, not tied to these rings' protocol.
- `tp-matrix` and `tp-cell` stay: they time these rings'
  protocol phase by phase, which only this crate can do.

## Build / test / install

```sh
cargo build -p tp_matrix

content.content:
## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

229:## Close-out shapes
230-
231-The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
232-[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
233-is one commit and lands as it is:
234-
235-- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
236-  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
237-  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
238-  by the landing fast-forward itself.
239-- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.
240-
241-Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
242-rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
243-shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).
244-
245-**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
246-whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
247-described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
248-trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
249-and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.
250-
251-## Read a change in gitk at full context
252-
253-gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
254-"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
255-is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:
256-
257-- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
258-  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
259-- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
260-  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
261-- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
262-  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.
263-
264-The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
265-together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:
266-
267-- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
268-- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".
269-
274:## Trapezoid close-out recipe
275-
276-The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
277-close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
278-trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
279-with Land's fast-forward.
280-
281-```
282-  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
283-                      \                    /
284-  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
285-```
286-
287-- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
288-  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
289-  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
290-- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
291-- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.
292-
293-1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
294-   order is the argument order.
295-2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
296-   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
297-   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
298-   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
299-3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
300-   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
301-   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
302-   `jj log --no-graph`.
303-
304-Details:
305-
306-- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
307-  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
308-- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
309-  fast-forward.
310-
311-Recovery:
312-
313-- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
314-  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
315-- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
316-  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
317-  recovery is forward-only.
318-- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
319-  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.

# Agent-files size

The line count of the agent-files, one row per landing, so the set's size is tracked over time.
Smaller is the quasi-goal: a rule stated once is shorter than a rule stated three times, and a
shrinking count is evidence the set is converging, while a growing one is a prompt to ask what
arrived as a paragraph that should have been a line. The count is not a rule, and a rule is never

    the L2 footprint the cycle expected at 1000 never shows.

    buffer the consumer's free just pushed, so the working
    set is the messages actually in flight, not the pool.

    the queue does.

content.content:
### feat: clearer tp_matrix counters and a tool map

#### Problem

`tp-pool` prints a count of the cordyceps consumer's `Inconsistent` retries, a normal cost of
Vyukov's queue already inside the row's ns/msg, as if it were a finding. The `fills` columns of all
four tools name a perf event rather than what it shows, cache lines pulled into a core from another
core's cache, so a table at an SMT pair, where nothing crosses, reads as a fault. The tp_matrix
README describes each tool alone and never says how their numbers relate, so which of them belongs
in iiac-perf cannot be read off it: `tp-matrix --depth 1,8,64,1024` and `tp-pool` share a depth
axis and measure different things. The mpsc-v0 skip message names a floor without saying which
flavor runs below it.

#### Solution

Drop the `Inconsistent` count and let the cordyceps consumer wait on it as on `Empty`. Label the
fill columns `xfills`, x-core cache-line fills, with a legend under each tool's table defining every
column, merge `tp-matrix`'s two tables into one, and reword the mpsc-v0 skip to name its floor and
mpsc-v1. Extend the tp_matrix README with a map of the tools against each other: shape, messages in
flight, what depth changes, what each reports, and the SMT reading.
##### docs: tp_matrix README maps the tools against each other

The README described each tool alone, in no set order, so which to run and how their numbers
relate was left to the reader.

* Nothing compared the tools.
  - A side-by-side table, then one section per tool in the table's order.
* The overview was one dense paragraph.
  - "The measurements" says in plain words what the tools do, with one bullet per tool, and that
    xfills near 0 at an SMT pair is expected.
* `tp-pool`'s depth reads like `tp-matrix`'s and is not.
  - The tp-pool section says depth throttles there and which cells come closest.

##### feat: clearer tp_matrix counters and a tool map closing

Closing out the cycle.

## Waiting

3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.

content.content:
### Segmented queue SPSC v3

Every ring is fixed-length and Full fails the send. The segment chain was designed for v1 in [SPSC
v1: seam-word ring](notes/ring-buffer-design.md#spsc-v1-seam-word-ring) and held until a ring
cleared the bar, v2 cleared it on 2026-09-07, so the layer goes on v2. The cycle, drafted on
2026-09-08 and not yet agreed, runs as `feat: segmented queue SPSC v3`:
- Solution: a `spsc::v3` sibling module whose queue is a chain of v2 ring segments, each one pool
  buffer holding a v2 region.
  - Geometry: `Queue::init(region, slot_size, seg_capacity, seg_count)` builds a `Pool` over the
    caller's region with buffer size `v2::region_size(slot_size, seg_capacity)` and `seg_count`
    buffers, takes the first segment, and splits into `Producer` and `Consumer`. Total capacity is
    the product, and the pool bound is the queue bound, so Full means the pool is exhausted.
  - Endpoints: the producer holds the `Pool` plus a v2 producer over its current segment, the
    consumer a `PoolResolver` plus a v2 consumer over its segment. The guards are v2's `WriteSlot`
    and `ReadSlot` re-exported, so the hot path inside a segment is v2's untouched.
  - Link word: word 0 of the segment header's `user` line holds the next segment's pool buffer
    index, sentinel `u32::MAX` for none. Not the free-stack word, which is buffer word 0 and
    doubles as the v2 magic, so a free scribbling it costs nothing.
  - Producer on Full: try the current segment once, on Full allocate a segment, `v2::Ring::init`
    it, store its index in the old segment's link with Release, move. Pool exhausted is the queue's
    Full, and the wait policy runs over both retries, the current segment first.
  - Consumer on Empty: try the current segment once, on Empty load the link with Acquire. A set
    link means the old segment is drained, since every commit in it happened before the link store
    and Empty says the slot at the consumer's position is uncommitted, so the consumer moves and
    frees the old segment. An unset link means the producer is still here, and the wait policy
    runs.
  - Pool change, the one the design note allowed: `alloc::<()>` already hands out a whole buffer,
    so add `BufSlot::as_mut_bytes` for the init and a crate-private buffer pointer on the resolver
    for the consumer's attach and free.
  - Held out: no `attach` this cycle. The endpoints are in-process, since resuming needs a queue
    control block holding both sides' current segment, a later entry if a consumer for it appears.
- Acceptance check: a test streaming across many segment boundaries with a pool smaller than the
  message count, at `M = 1` and larger, that afterwards finds every segment but the live one back
  in the pool, and the size sweep on the 3900X in the design note with v3 at `M = depth` matching
  v2 within run noise.
- Prediction, on record: within a segment v3 is v2. Each seam costs the producer an alloc CAS, the
  init's header and seq lines, and a link store, and the consumer a header line for the link, a
  free CAS on the shared pool line, and a cold prefetcher on the new buffer. At `M = 1` roughly
  three times v2's two lines per message, and the slope from `M = 64` down shows where the seam
  stops mattering. We think it is flat by `M = 8`.
- Ladder, multi-step on one topic bookmark:
  - `feat: segmented queue SPSC v3 opening`
  - `feat: bytes and a buffer pointer from a pool buffer`, the pool accessors with tests
  - `feat: spsc v3 segment chain`, the module, both endpoints, the link protocol, the tests above
    plus `M = 1`, u32 wrap, and a threaded stress with a two-buffer pool that forces the exhausted
    wait and the unset-link retry
  - `feat: spsc v3 in the measurement tools`, a flavor in `tp-cell`, `tp-matrix`, `tp-stream`, and
    the demo's sweep, with a segment-capacity knob. Depth stays the total capacity and the segment
    count is depth over `M`, so `M = depth` is the v2 baseline inside v3
  - `perf: sweep the segment size`, `M` from 1 to depth at depths 64 and 256 across the three
    pinned placements, the numbers into a new design-note section and the crate's default `M`
    chosen from them, the 7600X pasted in by the user
  - `feat: segmented queue SPSC v3 closing`, which deletes the Overflow FIFO entry this supersedes
- Decisions the user has not yet given: `Ring` stays v2 and v3 is reached by path as
  `spsc::v3::Queue`, attach deferred, trapezoid at close-out.
- supersedes Overflow FIFO if it lands.

content.content:
## Advancing X.Y.Z: patch by default

Which of the three numbers moves is not a classification problem
([why](rationale.md#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default)): **patch by default, minor by the user's call,
major by the project's promise.**

- **Patch by default**: every cycle advances `Z`, whatever it touched. Code or docs, large or small,
  none of it matters, so the choice costs no deliberation.
- **Minor is deliberate and rare**: the user names it at a cycle's opening when the change deserves
  a visible marker in the history, and the agent never infers it from a change's content or size.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its users.
  A project that makes that promise records it as its local edit of this rule, and absent one the
  default above governs.

## Grammar and storage

  that introduced it.
- **Spelling**: `vX.Y.Z` everywhere the agent-files version is written, the file name, an
  `agent-files` title, and vc-x1's output, so `agent-files v0.1.0` reads the same in all three. The
  `v` is the name-plus-version pair as cargo prints it (`bar v1.0.0`), and a tool's own banner stays
  bare (`vc-x1 0.82.0`), so a `v` number is the set's and a bare one the artifact's.
- **Proposals bump, adoptions copy**: a proposal cycle bumps it at the opening, advancing per

content.text:
You chose 0.16.0, and v3 follows the same pattern as v0 through v2. That pattern means:
- **Type names:** `spsc::v3::Ring` with `init` and `split`, plus `Producer`, `Consumer`, `WriteSlot`, and `ReadSlot`. It's `Ring`, not the draft's `Queue`.
- **Access:** reached by its explicit path. The crate default stays v2, so I won't repoint `spsc::{Ring, …}` unless you say so.

One part of "the same" is ambiguous: v0 through v2 all have an `attach`. I'll come back to that after the seam rule.

## The seam, step by step

**The players:**
- **Segments:** each segment is a v2 ring inside one pool buffer.
- **The link:** word 0 of a segment's user line holds the index of the next segment, or "none".
- **Who writes what:** only the producer writes the link, and only once per segment.

**Producer, when the current segment reports `Full`:**
1. Allocate a new buffer from the pool, and `init` a v2 ring in it.
2. Store the new buffer's index in the old segment's link.
3. Switch to the new segment. The producer never touches the old one again.

The key fact: **every commit to the old segment happens before step 2.** The producer only links after `Full`, and never writes to the old segment after linking.

**Consumer, when its current segment reports `Empty`:**

The draft said: load the link, and if it's set, the old segment is drained, so move and free it. Here's a timeline where that goes wrong:

| time | producer | consumer |
|---|---|---|
| t1 | | tries slot *p* in old segment: `Empty` |
| t2 | commits *p*, *p+1*, … until `Full` | |
| t3 | allocs new segment, stores link | |
| t4 | | loads link: set, so moves on and frees the old segment |

At t4, slots *p* onward in the old segment hold committed messages the consumer never read. Freeing the segment loses them. And if the producer reallocates that buffer, it overwrites them.

The `Empty` at t1 was true at t1, but by t4 it's stale.

**Fix: a second look.** When the link is set, try the old segment again before moving:
- **The link was set** means the store at t3 happened before the consumer's load at t4.
- **All commits precede the store,** so by t4 every message in the old segment is already visible.
- **So on the second try:**
  - **A message:** consume it normally and keep draining the old segment.
  - **Still `Empty`:** the old segment really is drained. Move to the new segment and free the old one.

That also keeps FIFO order: the consumer finishes the old segment completely before starting the new one.

**What the first `Empty` check still does:** it only decides whether to look at the link at all. The unset-link case (producer still writing here) goes to the wait policy, as the draft had it.

**The pool running out:** when the producer can't allocate, the result is the queue's `Full`. The producer retries its current segment first, because the consumer may have released slots in the meantime.

The plain version: the consumer must check the old segment one more time after it sees the link. The link proves the producer is finished there, but the earlier "empty" could have been read before the producer's last messages arrived.

Two questions:
1. Does the second-look rule hold up for you, or is there a case you want to walk through?
2. For attach: v0 through v2 each have one. For v3, attach needs a queue control block recording both sides' current segment. Should v3 get attach this cycle, matching v0 through v2, or keep the draft's deferral?

content.text:
Yes, that's a small change. The default is a single line in `src/spsc/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub use v2::{Consumer, Header, Producer, ReadSlot, Ring, WriteSlot};
```

`src/lib.rs` re-exports it at the crate root. It can point at v2 throughout development and switch to v3 in a late rung.

**What the switch touches.** Code that uses the crate-root `Ring` expects v2's surface:
- **`Ring::init(region, slot_size, capacity)` over a ring-sized region:** used by the README example, `examples/readme.rs`, and tests in `registry.rs` and `pool/v0`. v3's `init` takes a pool-sized region plus a segment capacity and count, so these calls won't compile against v3 unchanged.
- **`Ring::attach`:** the mpsc cross-kind tests use it (`use crate::Ring` in `mpsc/v0` and `mpsc/v1`). If v3 has no `attach`, the default loses it.
- **`Header`:** v2's ring header. v3 has a pool header plus one v2 header per segment, so nothing maps onto `Header` directly.

**How I'd handle it.** Add a rung after the perf sweep, so the default segment size `M` is already chosen: `feat: spsc v3 as the crate default`.
- **Repoint** the re-export to v3.
- **Tests:** those that are really about v2 geometry, like the registry, pool, and mpsc cross-kind tests, name `spsc::v2::Ring` explicitly.
- **README example and `examples/readme.rs`:** rewritten to show v3's `init`.
- **`Header`:** v3 either exports its own under that name, or the name leaves the default re-export. I'll bring the choice to you in that rung.

**How this bears on attach.** With v3 as the default, a v3 without `attach` means the crate-root `Ring` has no `attach`. That makes attach this cycle more attractive, though it costs the queue control block and a larger cycle.

Three things still open before the opening:
1. **Seam rule:** does the second look hold up for you?
2. **Attach:** should v3 get it this cycle, given it becomes the default?
3. **Default rung:** OK to add `feat: spsc v3 as the crate default` after the perf sweep?

content.text:
**Making v3 the default from the start.** Yes, that's a bit easier. One rung makes the switch, instead of two rungs editing the same call sites.
- **When:** it can't happen in the opening, because v3 doesn't exist yet. It would happen in the `feat: spsc v3 segment chain` rung. That same rung would move the v2-specific tests (registry, pool, mpsc cross-kind) to explicit `spsc::v2::Ring` paths, and rewrite the README example for v3's `init`.
- **Payoff:** every later rung builds against v3 as the default, so API awkwardness shows up early.
- **Measurement tools:** already name versions by path, so they aren't affected.
- **Default `M`:** the perf sweep's choice only matters if we add a convenience constructor. `init` takes the segment capacity explicitly, so nothing blocks on it.
- **Cost:** for a few rungs, the default is a young v3 on a draft bookmark. That seems fine to me.

**MPSC at the seam.** Your "CAS the link, first one wins, losers give their segments back to the pool" is the right starting shape, and it's lock-free. What changes is everything around the link:

- **Optimistic allocation vs claim-first.**
  - **Optimistic (yours):** every producer that hits `Full` allocates and inits a segment, then CASes the link from none to its own index. Losers free their segment and follow the winner's. That's lock-free, but under contention some allocs and inits are wasted, and it briefly takes extra pool buffers.
  - **Claim-first:** CAS a "linking" marker before allocating. Nothing is wasted, but a producer preempted while holding the claim stalls all the others. That's the same unbounded-stall problem the cordyceps `Inconsistent` spin has.
  - **Verdict:** I'd take optimistic.
- **A loser may find the pool empty.** The winner took the last buffer, so a loser's alloc fails. It should re-read the link before reporting `Full`, since the queue may have grown in the meantime.
- **The SPSC invariant breaks.** With one producer, every commit to the old segment happens before the link store. With several:
  - **A late commit:** one producer can claim the last slot of the old segment but not yet have committed it when another sees `Full` and links. The consumer's second look then sees an uncommitted slot, reads `Empty`, and moves on, losing that message.
  - **New claims:** worse, as the consumer releases slots in the old segment, producers that haven't noticed the link can claim new slots there.
- **What fixes that: seal, then link.** Before linking, a producer CASes a "sealed" bit into the old segment's claim index, so no one can claim there again. The consumer stops using `Empty` as its "drained" test. It drains until its position equals the sealed claim index, an exact count.
  - This works for SPSC too, and is stronger than the second look. It may be worth using in v3 so the MPSC version reuses the shape.
- **Freeing is where it gets hard.** In SPSC the producer has left the old segment for good before the consumer frees it. In MPSC, a slow producer may have read the old segment's address before the seal, then claim or commit into a buffer that was already freed and handed to someone else. That's a use-after-free, plus an ABA problem on the link's buffer index. The fix is some reclamation scheme: a generation number in the segment header that producers re-check after claiming, hazard pointers, or epochs. That's the real cost of MPSC segments, much more than the link CAS.

The plain version: switching the default early is easy and a little less work. For MPSC, racing to CAS the link is the right idea, but several producers also have to seal the old segment so nobody writes into it late. The hard part is making sure no slow producer is still using a segment when the consumer gives it back to the pool.

content.text:
Agreed. With one producer, v3 needs no CAS at the seam and no seal. The producer allocates, inits, stores the link with a plain store, and moves on. The consumer's second look is the only extra work, and it only happens at a seam. That keeps the hot path inside a segment exactly v2's, which is what the prediction on record expects.

**What SPSC should teach us for MPSC:**
- **Seam cost:** how much an alloc, init, and link store cost next to v2's two lines per message.
- **Pool traffic:** whether segment churn through the shared pool line shows up in the xfills.
- **Segment size:** how small `M` can go before the seams dominate.
- **Consumer hand-off:** the consumer attaching to a buffer it didn't create, and freeing it.

I'd write those findings into the design note's v3 section, and add a short "carried to MPSC" list there: optimistic CAS for the link, seal before link, and reclamation. The design lives on after the cycle while the MPSC thinking is still fresh.

content.text:
You're right, attach has nothing to do with versioning. They're separate questions:

- **Versioning** is which ring implementation you get. Users can always name one, `zc_ring_x1::spsc::v2::Ring` or `spsc::v3::Ring`, and if they don't, `zc_ring_x1::Ring` gives them the default. Adding v3 doesn't change that.
- **Attach** is a capability a ring version may have. `init` sets up a fresh ring in a memory region and writes its header. `attach` joins a ring that already exists in a region: say a second process that mapped the same shared memory, or a program resuming after a restart. It checks the header and continues where the ring left off. It exists in v0 through v2 because a ring's whole state lives in its region.

So the question is only whether v3 needs that capability now. Attaching to a v3 queue is harder, because its state is spread over a pool and a chain of segments. Something in the region has to record where each side currently is.

My recommendation is to leave attach out of v3 this cycle:
- **Anyone who needs attach** names `spsc::v2::Ring`, which keeps it. That's the versioning working as intended.
- **Code calling `zc_ring_x1::Ring::attach`** fails to compile once the default is v3, which is a clear signal to pick v2. Inside this crate, the only callers are the mpsc cross-kind tests, and they move to `spsc::v2::Ring` in the segment-chain rung anyway.
- **v3 attach** stays a Todo entry, for when someone actually needs it.

The plain version: versioning is which ring you use, and attach is whether a ring can reconnect to memory it was set up in earlier. v3 can skip reconnecting for now, and anyone who needs it can choose v2.

If that works for you, the plan is settled. The opening's first action is creating and publishing the `feat-segmented-queue-spsc-v3` bookmark at `main`, which needs your OK.
