1	//! Message pool: fixed-size buffers over a caller-provided
2	//! region, handed out through an intrusive LIFO free-stack —
3	//! the allocation half of the messaging layer, decoupling
4	//! "get a message" from "send it" (see the design doc's
5	//! "Messaging layer: pools and descriptor queues").
6	//!
7	//! - One `#[repr(C)]` [`PoolHeader`] spanning two cache lines
8	//!   (immutable geometry, free-stack head), followed by
9	//!   `buf_count` buffers of `buf_size` bytes each.
10	//! - The free-stack is intrusive with zero per-buffer
11	//!   overhead: a *free* buffer's first word holds the index
12	//!   of the next free buffer; an allocated buffer carries no
13	//!   header at all (in-buffer provenance is deferred — the
14	//!   descriptor is the travel form; see the design doc's
15	//!   "Descriptor and registry design (0.7.0)").
16	//! - One owning allocator pops ([`Pool::alloc`], `&mut self`
17	//!   as the in-process single-popper token); any holder
18	//!   frees ([`BufSlot::free`], the MPSC push side). The
19	//!   [`BufSlot`] guard does not borrow the pool, so any
20	//!   number of allocated buffers may be live at once —
21	//!   the decoupling the messaging layer exists for.
22	
23	use core::marker::PhantomData;
24	use core::mem::size_of;
25	use core::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};
26	use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, Ordering};
27	use zerocopy::{FromBytes, IntoBytes, KnownLayout};
28	
29	use crate::{CACHE_LINE_SIZE, CacheAligned, Error, check_type};
30	
31	/// `alloc` failed: no free buffer (or a peer-corrupted
32	/// free-stack index — validation fails toward exhaustion,
33	/// never toward handing out memory the pool doesn't own).
34	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
35	pub struct Exhausted;
36	
37	/// Layout marker written by [`Pool::init`]; rejects foreign
38	/// (including ring) regions on attach.
39	const POOL_MAGIC: u32 = 0x5A43_5031; // "ZCP1"
40	
41	/// Bumped on any change to the pool region layout.
42	const POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION: u32 = 1;
43	
44	/// Free-stack terminator: no next free buffer.
45	///
46	/// - Also why `buf_count < u32::MAX`: every valid index must
47	///   be distinguishable from the sentinel.
48	const NIL: u32 = u32::MAX;
49	
50	/// Control block at offset 0 of a pool region — two cache
51	/// lines: cold geometry, then the contended free-stack head.
52	///
53	/// - line 0: geometry, written by [`Pool::init`] with `magic`
54	///   last (`Release`), read-only thereafter. Cold: per-op
55	///   paths use the handle's snapshot.
56	/// - line 1: `first_free_idx`, CAS-contended by every freer and
57	///   the allocator — sole owner of its line.
58	/// - Every field is atomic for the same reason as the ring
59	///   [`Header`](crate::Header): a peer may be mapped at any
60	///   time, and scribbles must be garbage values, never UB.
61	#[repr(C)]
62	pub struct PoolHeader {
63	    /// Layout marker ([`POOL_MAGIC`]); stored last by init
64	    /// (`Release`), loaded first by attach (`Acquire`).
65	    magic: AtomicU32,
66	    /// Pool layout version ([`POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION`]).
67	    layout_version: AtomicU32,
68	    /// Buffer size in bytes — a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] multiple.
69	    buf_size: AtomicU32,
70	    /// Buffer count — nonzero, `< u32::MAX` ([`NIL`]).
71	    buf_count: AtomicU32,
72	    /// [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] this region was built with; attach
73	    /// validates it like the rest of the geometry.
74	    cache_line_size: AtomicU32,
75	    /// Free-stack head: index of the first free buffer, or
76	    /// [`NIL`] when the pool is exhausted.
77	    first_free_idx: CacheAligned<AtomicU32>,
78	}
79	
80	const _: () = assert!(size_of::<PoolHeader>() == 2 * CACHE_LINE_SIZE);
81	
82	/// A validated view over a pool region.
83	///
84	/// - Geometry is snapshotted out of the header at
85	///   init/attach: per-op paths never re-read fields a peer
86	///   could scribble on. Free-stack links live in shared
87	///   buffer memory and are validated at every pop instead.
88	pub struct Pool<'a> {
89	    /// The region's control block.
90	    header: &'a PoolHeader,
91	    /// Base of the buffer array
92	    /// (offset `size_of::<PoolHeader>()`).
93	    bufs: *mut u8,
94	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_size`.
95	    buf_size: u32,
96	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_count`.
97	    buf_count: u32,
98	    _region: PhantomData<&'a [u8]>,
99	}
100	
101	// SAFETY: the handle owns the allocator role; the shared
102	// state it touches (first_free_idx, next-links) is atomic,
103	// and buffer ownership is handed off with Release/Acquire
104	// ordering — same rationale as the ring endpoints.
105	unsafe impl Send for Pool<'_> {}
106	
107	impl<'a> Pool<'a> {
108	    /// Initialize a fresh region and return the pool over it,
109	    /// with every buffer on the free-stack.
110	    ///
111	    /// - `buf_size` — bytes per buffer, a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]
112	    ///   multiple.
113	    /// - `buf_count` — number of buffers, nonzero and
114	    ///   `< u32::MAX`.
115	    /// - The region must be [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]-aligned and at
116	    ///   least `size_of::<PoolHeader>() + buf_count *
117	    ///   buf_size` bytes.
118	    pub fn init(region: &'a mut [u8], buf_size: u32, buf_count: u32) -> Result<Self, Error> {
119	        validate_pool_geometry(buf_size, buf_count)?;
120	        let len = region.len();
121	        // Taken exactly once — same Stacked Borrows retag
122	        // hazard as Ring::init.
123	        let base = region.as_mut_ptr();
124	        let header = pool_header_ptr(base, len)?;
125	        if (len as u64) < pool_region_size(buf_size, buf_count) {
126	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
127	        }
128	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the PoolHeader checked
129	        // by pool_header_ptr; region is exclusively borrowed
130	        // for 'a; any byte pattern is a valid PoolHeader
131	        // (all-atomic fields, plain-byte padding).
132	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
133	        header
134	            .layout_version
135	            .store(POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION, Ordering::Relaxed);
136	        header.buf_size.store(buf_size, Ordering::Relaxed);
137	        header.buf_count.store(buf_count, Ordering::Relaxed);
138	        header
139	            .cache_line_size
140	            .store(CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32, Ordering::Relaxed);
141	        // SAFETY: in bounds — len >= header + buffers.
142	        let bufs = unsafe { base.add(size_of::<PoolHeader>()) };
143	        let pool = Pool {
144	            header,
145	            bufs,
146	            buf_size,
147	            buf_count,
148	            _region: PhantomData,
149	        };
150	        // Link every buffer into the free-stack: i -> i + 1,
151	        // last -> NIL, head -> 0.
152	        for i in 0..buf_count {
153	            let next = if i + 1 == buf_count { NIL } else { i + 1 };
154	            pool.next_buf_idx(i).store(next, Ordering::Relaxed);
155	        }
156	        pool.header.first_free_idx.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);
157	        // Published last: a peer that pre-mapped the region
158	        // must never observe the magic before the geometry it
159	        // validates (same handshake as Ring::init).
160	        pool.header.magic.store(POOL_MAGIC, Ordering::Release);
161	        Ok(pool)
162	    }
163	
164	    /// Attach to a pool region another process (or an earlier
165	    /// call) already initialized, validating its header.
166	    ///
167	    /// # Safety
168	    ///
169	    /// - `region` points to `len` bytes of memory that outlive
170	    ///   `'a`, genuinely shared and writable (e.g. a
171	    ///   `MAP_SHARED` mapping).
172	    /// - At most one attached handle acts as the pool's
173	    ///   allocator (single-popper contract); any handle may
174	    ///   free.
175	    pub unsafe fn attach(region: *mut u8, len: usize) -> Result<Self, Error> {
176	        let header = pool_header_ptr(region, len)?;
177	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the PoolHeader checked
178	        // by pool_header_ptr; caller guarantees the memory is
179	        // live and shared.
180	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
181	        // Acquire pairs with init's Release store of magic.
182	        if header.magic.load(Ordering::Acquire) != POOL_MAGIC {
183	            return Err(Error::BadMagic);
184	        }
185	        if header.layout_version.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION {
186	            return Err(Error::BadLayoutVersion);
187	        }
188	        if header.cache_line_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32 {
189	            return Err(Error::BadCacheLine);
190	        }
191	        // Snapshot geometry once; per-op paths never re-read.
192	        let buf_size = header.buf_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
193	        let buf_count = header.buf_count.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
194	        validate_pool_geometry(buf_size, buf_count)?;
195	        if (len as u64) < pool_region_size(buf_size, buf_count) {
196	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
197	        }
198	        // SAFETY: in bounds — len >= header + buffers.
199	        let bufs = unsafe { region.add(size_of::<PoolHeader>()) };
200	        Ok(Pool {
201	            header,
202	            bufs,
203	            buf_size,
204	            buf_count,
205	            _region: PhantomData,
206	        })
207	    }
208	
209	    /// Pop the first free buffer off the free-stack as an
210	    /// owned [`BufSlot`], or [`Exhausted`].
211	    ///
212	    /// - `&mut self` is the in-process single-popper token;
213	    ///   cross-process, at most one attached handle allocates
214	    ///   (see [`Pool::attach`]). The guard does **not** borrow
215	    ///   the pool — any number of allocated buffers may be
216	    ///   live at once; per-buffer exclusivity comes from the
217	    ///   free-stack protocol (each pop yields a distinct
218	    ///   index), not the borrow checker.
219	    /// - Validated pop: the head and its next-link live in
220	    ///   peer-writable memory, so both are bounds-checked;
221	    ///   corruption degrades to `Exhausted` (mirroring the
222	    ///   ring's fail-toward-`Full` occupancy check), never to
223	    ///   an out-of-bounds buffer.
224	    /// - A racing free moves the head and the CAS retries;
225	    ///   with a single popper an in-flight head node cannot be
226	    ///   removed underneath us, so there is no ABA hazard.
227	    /// - `T` geometry is asserted on each call (a mismatch is
228	    ///   a programming error, so it panics — same doctrine as
229	    ///   `reserve_slot_with`). A zero-sized `T` is legal and still
230	    ///   consumes a whole buffer: the buffer is the
231	    ///   allocation granule.
232	    pub fn alloc<T>(&mut self) -> Result<BufSlot<'a, T>, Exhausted>
233	    where
234	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
235	    {
236	        check_type::<T>(self.buf_size);
237	        loop {
238	            // Acquire pairs with free's Release CAS: seeing a
239	            // head index means seeing that buffer's next-link
240	            // store (and the freer's last writes) too.
241	            let head = self.header.first_free_idx.load(Ordering::Acquire);
242	            if head == NIL {
243	                return Err(Exhausted);
244	            }
245	            if head >= self.buf_count {
246	                return Err(Exhausted);
247	            }
248	            let next = self.next_buf_idx(head).load(Ordering::Relaxed);
249	            if next != NIL && next >= self.buf_count {
250	                return Err(Exhausted);
251	            }
252	            if self
253	                .header
254	                .first_free_idx
255	                .compare_exchange(head, next, Ordering::Acquire, Ordering::Relaxed)
256	                .is_ok()
257	            {
258	                return Ok(BufSlot {
259	                    header: self.header,
260	                    buf: self.buf_ptr(head),
261	                    idx: head,
262	                    _slot: PhantomData,
263	                });
264	            }
265	        }
266	    }
267	
268	    /// [`alloc`](Pool::alloc) with an injected wait policy:
269	    /// retry until a buffer frees up or the policy gives up.
270	    ///
271	    /// - `on_exhausted` is called after each failed attempt
272	    ///   with the attempt count (0-based, saturating);
273	    ///   returning `false` gives up → `Err(Exhausted)`.
274	    /// - See [`policy`](crate::policy) for shipped policies
275	    ///   and the composition model.
276	    pub fn alloc_with<T>(
277	        &mut self,
278	        mut on_exhausted: impl FnMut(u32) -> bool,
279	    ) -> Result<BufSlot<'a, T>, Exhausted>
280	    where
281	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
282	    {
283	        let mut attempt = 0u32;
284	        loop {
285	            match self.alloc::<T>() {
286	                Ok(buf_slot) => return Ok(buf_slot),
287	                Err(Exhausted) => {
288	                    if !on_exhausted(attempt) {
289	                        return Err(Exhausted);
290	                    }
291	                    attempt = attempt.saturating_add(1);
292	                }
293	            }
294	        }
295	    }
296	
297	    /// Buffer size in bytes (geometry snapshot).
298	    pub fn buf_size(&self) -> u32 {
299	        self.buf_size
300	    }
301	
302	    /// Buffer count (geometry snapshot).
303	    pub fn buf_count(&self) -> u32 {
304	        self.buf_count
305	    }
306	
307	    /// A non-allocating [`PoolResolver`] view of this pool,
308	    /// for registration in a
309	    /// [`PoolRegistry`](crate::PoolRegistry).
310	    ///
311	    /// - Derived from this handle (same provenance as its own
312	    ///   pointers), so no second region borrow and no Stacked
313	    ///   Borrows retag hazard — `init`/`attach` take the
314	    ///   region pointer exactly once.
315	    /// - Any number of views may exist; none can allocate, so
316	    ///   the single-popper contract stays with this handle.
317	    pub fn resolver(&self) -> PoolResolver<'a> {
318	        PoolResolver {
319	            header: self.header,
320	            bufs: self.bufs,
321	            buf_size: self.buf_size,
322	            buf_count: self.buf_count,
323	        }
324	    }
325	
326	    /// The next-free-buffer index cell of buffer `idx` — its
327	    /// first word, the intrusive free-stack link, meaningful
328	    /// only while the buffer is free.
329	    ///
330	    /// - Returns the atomic cell, not the value; symmetric
331	    ///   with the header's `first_free_idx`.
332	    /// - Callers pass `idx < buf_count` (validated pops /
333	    ///   init's linking loop), keeping the deref in bounds.
334	    fn next_buf_idx(&self, idx: u32) -> &AtomicU32 {
335	        let p = self.buf_ptr(idx) as *const AtomicU32;
336	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count keeps the buffer in the
337	        // region validated at init/attach; the base is
338	        // cache-line aligned and buf_size is a line multiple,
339	        // so the first word is 4-aligned; all peers access it
340	        // as an atomic.
341	        unsafe { &*p }
342	    }
343	
344	    /// Pointer to buffer `idx`; callers pass
345	    /// `idx < buf_count`.
346	    fn buf_ptr(&self, idx: u32) -> *mut u8 {
347	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count, so the offset stays inside
348	        // the buffer array validated at init/attach.
349	        unsafe { self.bufs.add(idx as usize * self.buf_size as usize) }
350	    }
351	}
352	
353	/// A non-allocating view over a pool: resolves validated
354	/// buffer indices to owned [`BufSlot`] guards on behalf of a
355	/// [`PoolRegistry`](crate::PoolRegistry).
356	///
357	/// - Created by [`Pool::resolver`]; carries the same header
358	///   ref, buffer base, and geometry snapshot as its pool.
359	/// - Cannot allocate — the single-popper token stays with the
360	///   owning [`Pool`] handle.
361	/// - Identifies its pool by header address (see
362	///   [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc)).
363	#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
364	pub struct PoolResolver<'a> {
365	    /// The pool's control block.
366	    header: &'a PoolHeader,
367	    /// Base of the buffer array (copy of [`Pool::bufs`]).
368	    bufs: *mut u8,
369	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_size`.
370	    buf_size: u32,
371	    /// Snapshot of `header.buf_count`.
372	    buf_count: u32,
373	}
374	
375	// SAFETY: the view is read-only over its own fields; the only
376	// shared-memory mutation reachable through it is the minted
377	// guards' free CAS, which is the free-stack's any-thread MPSC
378	// push side. Allocation (the single-popper role) is not
379	// reachable from a resolver.
380	unsafe impl Send for PoolResolver<'_> {}
381	// SAFETY: all methods take &self and touch shared state only
382	// through atomics (as above), so concurrent use from multiple
383	// threads adds no non-atomic shared access.
384	unsafe impl Sync for PoolResolver<'_> {}
385	
386	impl<'a> PoolResolver<'a> {
387	    /// The pool's header address — its identity for registry
388	    /// lookups.
389	    pub(crate) fn header_ptr(&self) -> *const PoolHeader {
390	        self.header
391	    }
392	
393	    /// Buffer count (geometry snapshot).
394	    pub(crate) fn buf_count(&self) -> u32 {
395	        self.buf_count
396	    }
397	
398	    /// Buffer size in bytes (geometry snapshot).
399	    pub(crate) fn buf_size(&self) -> u32 {
400	        self.buf_size
401	    }
402	
403	    /// Mint the owned guard for buffer `idx`.
404	    ///
405	    /// # Safety
406	    ///
407	    /// - The caller has validated `idx < buf_count` and `T`'s
408	    ///   geometry against this pool.
409	    /// - The caller holds the buffer's ownership (the index
410	    ///   came from a consumed guard via
411	    ///   [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc),
412	    ///   arrived with happens-before ordering, and is resolved
413	    ///   exactly once) — minting a second live guard for one
414	    ///   buffer aliases `&mut T`.
415	    pub(crate) unsafe fn slot_from_idx<T>(&self, idx: u32) -> BufSlot<'a, T>
416	    where
417	        T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout,
418	    {
419	        // SAFETY: idx < buf_count (caller contract), so the
420	        // offset stays inside the buffer array validated at
421	        // init/attach.
422	        let buf = unsafe { self.bufs.add(idx as usize * self.buf_size as usize) };
423	        BufSlot {
424	            header: self.header,
425	            buf,
426	            idx,
427	            _slot: PhantomData,
428	        }
429	    }
430	}
431	
432	/// An allocated buffer, owned until [`free`](BufSlot::free):
433	/// `DerefMut` to use it as a `T` in place.
434	///
435	/// - Does not borrow the [`Pool`] — hold any number, as long
436	///   as you like; getting a buffer implies nothing about
437	///   when (or whether) it is sent or freed.
438	/// - Dropping without `free` leaks the buffer until the pool
439	///   is re-initialized (the abandon analog of the ring's
440	///   guards, with the opposite consequence).
441	pub struct BufSlot<'p, T> {
442	    /// The pool's control block (for the free CAS).
443	    header: &'p PoolHeader,
444	    /// Base of the owned buffer. Raw, and references are
445	    /// minted per access — same aliasing rationale as the
446	    /// ring guards.
447	    buf: *mut u8,
448	    /// This buffer's index (the value free pushes).
449	    idx: u32,
450	    /// The guard acts as a `&mut T` into the region.
451	    _slot: PhantomData<&'p mut T>,
452	}
453	
454	// SAFETY: the guard owns its buffer exclusively (the pop
455	// removed it from every shared structure); free's CAS is the
456	// only shared-state touch and is properly ordered.
457	unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for BufSlot<'_, T> {}
458	
459	impl<T> Deref for BufSlot<'_, T> {
460	    type Target = T;
461	    /// Read access to the buffer as a `T`.
462	    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
463	        // SAFETY: buf is in-bounds and cache-line aligned
464	        // (validated geometry), any byte pattern is a valid T
465	        // (FromBytes bound at alloc), and the pop gave this
466	        // guard sole ownership until free.
467	        unsafe { &*(self.buf as *const T) }
468	    }
469	}
470	
471	impl<T> DerefMut for BufSlot<'_, T> {
472	    /// Write access to the buffer as a `T`.
473	    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
474	        // SAFETY: as in deref; &mut self gives exclusivity of
475	        // the minted reference.
476	        unsafe { &mut *(self.buf as *mut T) }
477	    }
478	}
479	
480	impl<T> BufSlot<'_, T> {
481	    /// The owning pool's header address — matched against a
482	    /// registry entry's [`PoolResolver::header_ptr`] by
483	    /// [`PoolRegistry::into_desc`](crate::PoolRegistry::into_desc).
484	    pub(crate) fn header_ptr(&self) -> *const PoolHeader {
485	        self.header
486	    }
487	
488	    /// This buffer's index (the descriptor payload).
489	    pub(crate) fn idx(&self) -> u32 {
490	        self.idx
491	    }
492	
493	    /// Push the buffer back onto the pool's free-stack.
494	    ///
495	    /// - Any holder may free — this is the free-stack's MPSC
496	    ///   push side; only allocation is single-popper.
497	    /// - The CAS retries only when another free (or the
498	    ///   allocator's pop) moves the head first.

content.text:
I'd keep it as `pool::v0`. Here's my reasoning.

**What a new `vN` means in this crate.** A sibling version gets added when the region layout or the protocol changes, and the old one stays alive for comparison. spsc v1 moved the seq words, v2 moved the seq into the slot, and mpsc v1 changed the seq values. Each one changes how memory is laid out or how the two sides agree.

**What this rung changes:**
- **Region layout:** unchanged, so `POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION` is still 1. A pool built by the old code and one built by the new code are byte-for-byte the same.
- **Protocol:** the free-stack protocol is untouched.
- **API:** additions only. `BufSlot`'s new field lives in the in-process guard, not in shared memory.
- **Callers:** nothing that already uses the pool changes.

A `pool::v1` would copy about 950 lines to add two accessors, and the two copies would have nothing to compare.

**If it were bumped anyway, it should be v1, not v3.** Each module family numbers its own versions: spsc is at v2, mpsc at v1, pool at v0. Matching pool to spsc's v3 would suggest the two change together, and they don't. The pool also serves the descriptor rings and cordyceps.

**When a pool v1 would make sense:**
- **MPSC segments:** the reclamation problem from our MPSC discussion. A generation tag in each buffer would let a slow producer detect that its segment was freed and reused, and that changes the pool's layout.
- **Batch alloc/free:** the "Batch alloc/free demo" Todo, if it needs a different free-stack protocol.

The plain version: the pool just gained two small accessors. The memory layout and the rules are unchanged, so it stays `v0`. A new version is for when the layout or protocol changes, and if the pool ever gets one, it would be `v1`, since the pool numbers its versions separately from spsc.

content.text:
I agree that a segment is an ordinary pool allocation, and the pool shouldn't need to know segments exist. Neither accessor in this rung is segment-specific, but they do change the pool's API, so here's what v3 needs from the pool and how it could get it without any pool change.

**What v3 needs.** A plain `alloc` already covers the allocation itself: v3 allocates as `()`, and `free` covers returning a segment. Two things are missing:
1. **The segment's bytes.** The producer has to init a v2 ring over the whole buffer. A `BufSlot<()>` only hands out a `&mut ()`, which covers zero bytes, not the buffer.
2. **An address from an index.** The consumer learns the next segment from the link, which is an index. It has to find that buffer and join the ring there.

A zero-sized `T` can't provide either one legally. A pointer taken from a `&mut ()` is only permitted to touch zero bytes, so widening it to the whole buffer is undefined behavior under Rust's aliasing rules, and Miri would flag it.

**Doing it with no pool change.** v3's `init` receives the whole region itself. So:
- **Region pointer:** v3 takes the region's base pointer once, and every address comes from that one pointer.
  - **Pool:** built over the region from that pointer.
  - **Segment addresses:** computed as base, plus the pool header's size, plus index times buffer size.
- **The index:** from the existing crate-private `BufSlot::idx()`.
- **Freeing:** the consumer builds a guard from the index with the existing crate-private `PoolResolver::slot_from_idx`, then calls the normal `free`.

Nothing in `src/pool/` changes, and this rung disappears from the ladder. The cost is that v3 knows how the pool lays out its buffers: header first, then evenly sized buffers. That layout is pinned by `POOL_LAYOUT_VERSION`, and it lives in the same crate.

**Keeping the two accessors.** The pool changes, but only by adding code, and each accessor holds its own unsafe code. v3 then doesn't need to know the pool's layout.

I lean toward doing it with no pool change, because it matches your view and removes a rung. I'd write a comment in v3 naming the layout assumption, and add a test that fails if the pool's buffer addresses ever stop matching that formula.

message.content: When an entity allocates from the pool is receives information about it's location and size and a "zero-copy" cast from T to that allocated space must be safe. Now that allocated segement may have interior T's and those should use "zero-copy" to cast to those types, thoughts only.

content.text:
That principle helps, and I think it settles the question.

**What it means for the pool.** An allocation is bytes: a location and a size. Any typed view over them is a zero-copy cast that the type system checks, whether it's the whole buffer as one `T` or `T`s inside it. zerocopy provides that check:
- **The `T` bounds:** `T: FromBytes + IntoBytes + KnownLayout` means every byte pattern is a valid `T`, so the bytes can never produce a bad value.
- **Size and alignment:** `T::mut_from_bytes` or `mut_from_prefix` check both at runtime, and return an error rather than creating a bad reference.
- **Inner `T`s:** slice to the offset, then cast. An offset that isn't aligned for `T` becomes an error, not undefined behavior.

**What the pool does today.** `BufSlot<T>` fixes one `T` when you allocate and lets you `Deref` to it. That's the "whole buffer as `T`" case, but the bytes themselves are never available, so inner `T`s at other offsets can't be reached safely. Under your principle, the bytes are the basic thing the pool hands out, and the typed view is a convenience layered on top.

**What that does to this rung:**
- **`BufSlot::as_mut_bytes` stays.** It isn't a segment-specific addition. It's the location-and-size the principle says an allocation should come with, and every zero-copy cast is built on it.
- **`PoolResolver::buf_ptr` goes.** The consumer doesn't need a raw pointer. It turns the link's index back into a guard with the existing `slot_from_idx::<()>`, calls `as_mut_bytes`, and joins the v2 ring over those bytes. No raw address leaves the pool, and the v3 "knows the pool layout" workaround isn't needed either.
- **v2's `Ring::init` and `attach` are already this pattern.** They take bytes and check alignment and size before laying the header and slots over them. Inside the ring, `reserve_slot_with::<T>` is the zero-copy cast to each slot's `T`. A segment is bytes from the pool, and a ring inside it validates its own layout.
- **Possibly `as_bytes(&self)` as well**, for read-only views, so the pair is complete.

**A bigger version of this.** An untyped `BufSlot` that holds only bytes, where every typed view is a cast (`as_mut::<T>()`, `as_mut_prefix::<T>()`), would follow the principle all the way. But it changes every pool call site, including the descriptor rings, the demo, and `tp-pool`. I'd make that a Todo entry, not part of this cycle.

**One caution.** zerocopy's cast needs `IntoBytes` for write access, and a type with atomic fields, like v2's header, may not meet the bounds for a plain safe cast. We think that's why v2's `init` does its own validated cast. So a structure with shared atomics keeps its own validation step, while plain message types use zerocopy directly.

The plain version: a pool allocation should just be "these bytes, this big", and safe zero-copy casts give you typed views of the whole thing or parts of it. `as_mut_bytes` is exactly that, so it stays. The raw-pointer accessor isn't needed: the consumer can get a segment's bytes from its index through the pool's existing guard.

message.content: We've been using zero-copy and we've been mutating allocations returned by the pool. Why do we need as-mut_bytes now and not before?

lastPrompt: We've been using zero-copy and we've been mutating allocations returned by the pool. Why do we need as-mut_bytes now and not before?

content.text:
Because until now, what we put in a pool buffer always had a size fixed at compile time. A v3 segment's size is only known at runtime.

**How the existing code gets zero-copy access.** Every use allocates as a concrete `T`, and `BufSlot<T>`'s `DerefMut` gives `&mut T` over the buffer, a checked zero-copy cast:
- **Descriptor rings and the demo:** `Msg { seq }` and similar fixed structs.
- **tp-pool's cordyceps row:** `RawBuf([u8; CACHE_LINE_SIZE])`, a byte array whose length is a constant. The `Node` is then laid over those 64 bytes.
- **Common thread:** `size_of::<T>()` is known when the code compiles, and `check_type` checks it against the pool's buffer size.

**Why v3 is different.** A segment holds a whole v2 ring, whose size is `v2::region_size(slot_size, seg_capacity)`. Both values are arguments to `v3::Ring::init`, so the byte count is only known at runtime:
- **`[u8; N]` doesn't work:** `N` must be a compile-time constant.
- **`[u8]` doesn't work:** it's unsized, and `alloc::<T>` needs a sized `T`.
- **v2's `Ring::init` takes `&mut [u8]` anyway,** not a `T`, because a ring is itself a runtime-sized layout: a header, then *capacity* slots.

So no `T` describes a segment, and the typed `Deref` path can't hand v3 the bytes. `as_mut_bytes` is the untyped version of the same zero-copy access, with its length taken from the pool's runtime buffer size.

**When it wouldn't be needed.** If v3's segment size were a compile-time constant (for example, a const generic for the segment's byte size), v3 could allocate `BufSlot<[u8; SEG_BYTES]>` and pass `as_mut_slice()` to `Ring::init`, exactly as the cordyceps row does with `RawBuf`. That would fix `M` and the slot size when v3 is compiled, and give up the runtime `seg_capacity` argument the sweep relies on to vary `M`.

The plain version: everything we stored in the pool so far had a size known at compile time, so casting the buffer to that type was enough. A v3 segment's size depends on arguments passed at runtime, so no fixed type fits it, and v3 needs the buffer as plain bytes of the buffer's actual length.

content.text:
Not a size parameter, I think. But the question points at the right design.

**Why a size parameter adds nothing.** Every buffer in a pool has the same size, `buf_size`, set at `Pool::init`. An allocation always hands out a whole buffer, so there's no size to choose. A `size` argument could only be checked against `buf_size`, and `alloc::<T>` already does that with `size_of::<T>()`. The buffer's size is already a runtime value, the pool's. What's compile-time is the *view* `alloc::<T>` puts on it.

**What your earlier principle suggests.** "Allocation gives location and size, and typed access is a safe zero-copy cast" would split `alloc` in two:
- **`alloc()` is untyped.** It returns a guard that is just the buffer: its address, its `buf_size`, its index, and `free`. No `T`.
- **Typed access is a cast on that guard, when you need it:**
  - `as_mut::<T>()` for the whole buffer as a `T`.
  - `as_mut_prefix::<T>()`, or a cast at an offset, for `T`s inside the buffer.
  - The byte slice itself, for runtime-sized layouts like a v2 ring.
- **Where the check moves.** The size and alignment check moves from `alloc` to the cast, which is where it actually matters. And one buffer could then hold several different `T`s at different offsets, which today's `BufSlot<T>` can't do.

**What today's typed `alloc::<T>` still gives you:**
- **Deref convenience:** `buf.seq = 1` works directly.
- **An early check:** a `T` that doesn't fit panics at `alloc`, not later at a cast.
- **Typed descriptors:** the registry's `into_desc::<T>` and `resolve::<T>` carry the type through.

**How it could look with both.** Untyped `alloc()` becomes the primitive, and `alloc::<T>()` stays as a thin wrapper, alloc plus cast, so existing call sites don't change. Then:
- **v3** uses `alloc()` and the byte slice.
- **Message code** keeps `alloc::<T>()`.
- **This rung's `as_mut_bytes`** is the untyped guard's byte accessor, exposed a bit early.

**Where to do it.** Restructuring the guard touches every call site from my last answer, plus the registry's typed descriptors. I'd keep this cycle to `as_mut_bytes`, the smallest step consistent with that design, and add a Todo entry: "Untyped pool allocation with zero-copy views", describing the split.

The plain version: the pool's buffer size is already fixed at runtime, so passing a size wouldn't change anything. The cleaner idea is that `alloc` hands back plain bytes, and you cast them to whatever types you need. That's a bigger reshaping, so I'd note it as a Todo and keep only the byte accessor for now.

content.text:
That changes my answer: with size classes, a size argument means something.

**How the layers could fit:**
- **A fixed-size pool, like today's `Pool`,** hands out untyped buffers of its one `buf_size`. Inside a single pool there's still no size to choose.
- **A segmented pool** holds several sub-pools of different buffer sizes. Its `alloc(size)` picks the smallest sub-pool whose buffers fit `size`, and returns that buffer's location and its *actual* size, which may be larger than asked.
- **Typed access** is sugar on top. `alloc::<T>()` becomes `alloc(size_of::<T>())` followed by a zero-copy cast, and `T`s inside a buffer are casts on its bytes.
- **Alignment** stays free: every buffer starts on a cache line, so any `T` aligned to 64 bytes or less fits.

**What's already in place.** A descriptor is `Desc { pool_id, buf_idx }`, and a `PoolRegistry<N>` holds several pools. So a sub-pool can be its own registered pool, a descriptor already names which sub-pool a buffer came from, and `free` already goes back to the pool the guard came from. Size classes grow on top of the registry without changing the descriptor.

**What it means for this cycle:**
- **`as_mut_bytes` still fits.** A size-class allocation returns bytes of the chosen class's size, which is exactly this accessor.
- **A question about v3's `init`.** The draft has `v3::Ring::init(region, slot_size, seg_capacity, seg_count)` build its own private `Pool`. With app-designed pools, "a segment is just another pool allocation" points toward v3 taking a pool (or a sub-pool) the app provides, sized for `v2::region_size(slot_size, M)`, rather than owning one:
  - **v3 owns its pool:** matches v0 through v2's `init(region, …)` shape. Simple, and the queue bound is the pool bound. But v3's segments can't share memory with anything else.
  - **v3 takes an app pool:** matches your design. Several queues can draw segments from one sub-pool, and the app decides the sizes. But the queue bound becomes "whatever the pool has left", and `init` stops looking like v0 through v2's.
- **The segmented pool itself** is its own cycle, and it would include untyped `alloc` with typed casts. I'd file it as one Todo entry, "Segmented pools: size-class sub-pools with untyped allocation", recording the layering above.

The plain version: with pools of several buffer sizes, `alloc` does need a size, to pick which sub-pool to allocate from, and typed allocation becomes a cast on top. The descriptor and registry already support several pools. The open question for v3 is whether it keeps a private pool, as the plan says, or takes segments from a pool the app sets up.

content.text:
Yes, on both counts.

**Today.** Every existing caller is unchanged: the SPSC and MPSC descriptor paths, the registry, the demo, `tp-pool`, the examples, and the tests. `alloc::<T>()` still checks `T` against the buffer size and returns a `BufSlot<T>` that derefs to `T`, exactly as before. Under the hood, `alloc::<T>` and `alloc_bytes` are siblings: both call the same private `pop`, and they differ only in the view the guard carries.

**Later, with the Segmented pools Todo.** The layering flips so that bytes are the primitive:
- **The bytes call:** `alloc(size)`, the size-class version of `alloc_bytes`, picks a sub-pool and returns the buffer's bytes.
- **The typed call:** `alloc::<T>()` becomes that call with `size_of::<T>()`, followed by a checked conversion from the bytes guard to a `BufSlot<T>`, a zero-copy cast of the guard.
- **Callers:** still unchanged, since the typed call keeps its signature.

Doing the flip now would just route `alloc::<T>` through `alloc_bytes` plus a cast instead of calling `pop` directly. With a single buffer size it changes nothing, so I'd leave it for the segmented-pool cycle, where the size argument gives it a purpose.

The plain version: nobody else has to change. For now the typed and bytes versions share the same internals, and once pools have several sizes, the typed version will become a thin layer over the bytes version.

1	//! Zero-copy no_std SPSC ring buffer over a caller-provided
2	//! memory region, per [notes/ring-buffer-design.md]:
3	//!
4	//! - One `#[repr(C)]` [`Header`] spanning four cache lines
5	//!   (immutable geometry, producer index, consumer index, app
6	//!   user words), followed by M slots of N bytes.
7	//! - Indices are free-running `AtomicU32`s, masked only at slot
8	//!   access; full is `p - c == M`, no sacrificial slot.
9	//! - Messages move in place: the producer writes through a
10	//!   [`WriteSlot`] `&mut T`, the consumer reads through a
11	//!   [`ReadSlot`] `&T` — zerocopy traits bound `T`, no
12	//!   serialization step. Each side reserves at most one slot at
13	//!   a time; the guard holds the endpoint borrow until commit /
14	//!   release (or drop).
15	//! - The SPSC protocol lives in the `spsc` module; a
16	//!   multi-producer sibling, [`MpscRing`], lives in the
17	//!   `mpsc` module (gated on CAS support) — see its module
18	//!   docs for the claim/seq protocol and closure-send API.
19	//!   Primitive modules hold versioned sibling implementations
20	//!   (`spsc::v0`, …) behind per-module default-version
21	//!   re-exports; this crate root re-exports the defaults.
22	//!
23	//! [notes/ring-buffer-design.md]: https://github.com/winksaville/zc-ring-x1/blob/main/notes/ring-buffer-design.md
24	
25	#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)]
26	
27	use core::mem::{align_of, size_of};
28	use core::sync::atomic::AtomicU32;
29	
30	// The MPSC ring needs CAS (the claim), so it is gated; the
31	// SPSC ring protocol stays load/store-only. (The pool's
32	// free-stack also uses CAS and predates the gate — see
33	// notes/bugs.md.)
34	#[cfg(target_has_atomic = "32")]
35	pub mod mpsc;
36	pub mod policy;
37	pub mod pool;
38	mod registry;
39	pub mod spsc;
40	
41	#[cfg(target_has_atomic = "32")]
42	pub use mpsc::{MpscConsumer, MpscHeader, MpscProducer, MpscReadSlot, MpscRing, mpsc_region_size};
43	pub use pool::{BufSlot, Exhausted, Pool, PoolHeader, PoolResolver};
44	pub use registry::{Desc, PoolId, PoolRegistry, RegistryError};
45	pub use spsc::{Consumer, Header, Producer, ReadSlot, Ring, WriteSlot};
46	
47	/// Cache-line size the layout is built around.
48	///
49	/// - Slot size must be a multiple of this; slots and the region
50	///   itself must be aligned to it.
51	pub const CACHE_LINE_SIZE: usize = 64;
52	
53	/// Number of `AtomicU32` words in the header's app-owned
54	/// `user` line.
55	pub const USER_WORDS: usize = 16;
56	
57	/// `reserve_slot_with` / `send_with` failed: every slot holds
58	/// an uncommitted-or-unread message.
59	///
60	/// - Shared by the ring primitives (SPSC reserve, MPSC send) —
61	///   defined in the crate core so no primitive depends on a
62	///   sibling's version module for its error type.
63	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
64	pub struct Full;
65	
66	/// `reserve_slot_with` failed: no unread messages.
67	///
68	/// - Shared by the ring primitives' consumer endpoints — see
69	///   [`Full`] for why it lives in the crate core.
70	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
71	pub struct Empty;
72	
73	/// Cache-line-aligned wrapper granting its field sole
74	/// ownership of the line.
75	///
76	/// - `repr(align(N))` accepts only an integer literal — it
77	///   cannot name [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] — so the `64` is written out
78	///   and a const assert ties them back together.
79	#[repr(C, align(64))]
80	struct CacheAligned<T>(T);
81	
82	const _: () = assert!(align_of::<CacheAligned<AtomicU32>>() == CACHE_LINE_SIZE);
83	
84	impl<T> core::ops::Deref for CacheAligned<T> {
85	    type Target = T;
86	    /// Access the wrapped value.
87	    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
88	        &self.0
89	    }
90	}
91	
92	/// Errors from region validation — [`Ring::init`] /
93	/// [`Ring::attach`] and [`Pool::init`] / [`Pool::attach`].
94	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
95	pub enum Error {
96	    /// Region is not [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]-aligned.
97	    Misaligned,
98	    /// Region is smaller than header + slots/buffers.
99	    TooSmall,
100	    /// Slot size is zero or not a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] multiple.
101	    BadSlotSize,
102	    /// Capacity is zero, not a power of two, over the ring's
103	    /// cap, or under its floor (the MPSC v0 ring's is 2).
104	    BadCapacity,
105	    /// Pool: buffer size is zero or not a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]
106	    /// multiple.
107	    BadBufSize,
108	    /// Pool: buffer count is zero or `u32::MAX` (the
109	    /// free-stack NIL sentinel).
110	    BadBufCount,
111	    /// Attach: magic mismatch — not a region of the expected
112	    /// kind.
113	    BadMagic,
114	    /// Attach: layout version mismatch.
115	    BadLayoutVersion,
116	    /// Attach: region built with a different [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`].
117	    BadCacheLine,
118	}
119	
120	/// Check `T` fits a slot; called once per `reserve_slot_with`
121	/// (both endpoints).
122	///
123	/// - Panics on a type-geometry mismatch — that is a programming
124	///   error, not a runtime condition.
125	fn check_type<T>(slot_size: u32) {
126	    assert!(size_of::<T>() <= slot_size as usize, "T larger than slot");
127	    assert!(
128	        core::mem::align_of::<T>() <= CACHE_LINE_SIZE,
129	        "T alignment exceeds slot alignment"
130	    );
131	}
132	
133	/// Non-panicking form of [`check_type`], for descriptor
134	/// resolve — there the pool compared against is selected by
135	/// untrusted input, which must not be able to select a panic.
136	fn type_fits<T>(slot_size: u32) -> bool {
137	    size_of::<T>() <= slot_size as usize && core::mem::align_of::<T>() <= CACHE_LINE_SIZE
138	}
139	
140	/// Pointer to the slot for free-running index `idx`.
141	///
142	/// - Returned range is `slot_size` bytes, cache-line aligned
143	///   (base is, and slot_size is a line multiple).
144	fn slot_ptr(slots: *mut u8, idx: u32, mask: u32, slot_size: u32) -> *mut u8 {
145	    let pos = (idx & mask) as usize;
146	    // SAFETY: pos < capacity, so the offset is inside the slot
147	    // array validated at init/attach.
148	    unsafe { slots.add(pos * slot_size as usize) }
149	}

1	//! SPSC ring v2: the in-slot seq, per the design doc's "SPSC
2	//! v2: in-slot seq ring" section.
3	//!
4	//! - v1's protocol with the seq moved into the slot it
5	//!   publishes: every slot opens with a crate-owned
6	//!   [`SLOT_HEADER_BYTES`] header holding the seq word, and the
7	//!   user's message sits behind it in the same cache line. The
8	//!   commit store and the message it publishes then travel on
9	//!   one line, where v1 moves the slot line and, amortised, the
10	//!   seq line.
11	//! - Same region shape as v0, a four-line [`Header`] then the
12	//!   slots, and no seq array. `region_size` is header plus
13	//!   slots.
14	//! - The slot contract changes: `T` must fit `slot_size -
15	//!   SLOT_HEADER_BYTES` and align to at most
16	//!   `SLOT_HEADER_BYTES`, checked at every reserve as the other
17	//!   rings check theirs.
18	//! - Own magic and layout version, so cross-attaching fails
19	//!   toward [`Error::BadMagic`]. Load/store only, `capacity`
20	//!   any power of two down to 1, committed `pos + M + 1`, all
21	//!   as v1.
22	//! - The seq's width is [`Seq`], one alias, so the u32 against
23	//!   native-width measurement is a one-line flip.
24

26	use core::mem::{align_of, size_of};

43	/// of the other rings' layout versions.
44	const LAYOUT_VERSION: u32 = 1;
45	
46	/// Capacity bound: `2^30`, as v1 and the MPSC ring.
47	const MAX_CAPACITY: u32 = 1 << 30;
48	
49	/// Bytes the crate owns at the front of every slot: the seq
50	/// word first, the rest reserved.
51	///
52	/// - Sixteen rather than the seq's own width, so the seq can be
53	///   u32 or u64 without moving the body, and so a body may
54	///   align to 16.
55	/// - The body starts here, and a slot of N bytes carries
56	///   `N - SLOT_HEADER_BYTES` bytes of message.
57	pub const SLOT_HEADER_BYTES: usize = 16;
58	
59	/// The seq word's atomic type, the one place its width is
60	/// chosen.
61	///
62	/// - `AtomicU32` is the v1 width, the baseline.
63	/// - `AtomicU64` is the native width on the machines measured,
64	///   the other arm of the width probe.
65	pub type Seq = AtomicU32;
66	
67	/// The integer the seq holds, [`Seq`]'s plain form.
68	pub type SeqInt = u32;
69	
70	const _: () = assert!(size_of::<Seq>() <= SLOT_HEADER_BYTES);
71	const _: () = assert!(align_of::<Seq>() <= SLOT_HEADER_BYTES);
72	const _: () = assert!(SLOT_HEADER_BYTES < CACHE_LINE_SIZE);
73	
74	/// The crate-owned head of every slot.
75	///
76	/// - `seq` at offset 0, the protocol word.
77	/// - The rest reserved, zeroed by init and never read.
78	#[repr(C)]
79	pub struct SlotHeader {
80	    /// The slot's seq word: claimable at `pos`, committed at
81	    /// `pos + M + 1`, released at `pos + M`.
82	    seq: Seq,
83	    /// Reserved, so a wider seq or a later field has room.
84	    _reserved: [u8; SLOT_HEADER_BYTES - size_of::<Seq>()],
85	}
86	
87	const _: () = assert!(size_of::<SlotHeader>() == SLOT_HEADER_BYTES);
88	
89	/// Widen a free-running u32 index to the seq's integer.
90	///
91	/// - The indices stay u32 and wrap there, so the seq holds the
92	///   same values at either width, and a wider seq changes the
93	///   store's width alone.
94	fn seq_of(idx: u32) -> SeqInt {
95	    idx as SeqInt
96	}
97	
98	/// Control block at offset 0 of a v2 region, v1's four-line
99	/// shape as its own type.
100	///
101	/// - line 0: geometry, written by [`Ring::init`] with `magic`
102	///   last (`Release`), read-only thereafter.
103	/// - line 1: `producer_idx`, the producer's private resume
104	///   state.
105	/// - line 2: `consumer_idx`, the consumer's, likewise private.
106	/// - line 3: `user`, app-owned scratch, the v0 contract.
107	/// - Every field is atomic: the region may be mapped by a
108	///   peer at any time.
109	#[repr(C)]
110	pub struct Header {
111	    /// Layout marker ([`MAGIC`]): stored last by init
112	    /// (`Release`), loaded first by attach (`Acquire`).
113	    magic: AtomicU32,
114	    /// Layout version ([`LAYOUT_VERSION`]).
115	    layout_version: AtomicU32,
116	    /// Slot size N in bytes, a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] multiple.
117	    slot_size: AtomicU32,
118	    /// Slot count M, a power of two `<= 2^30`.
119	    capacity: AtomicU32,
120	    /// [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`] this region was built with.
121	    cache_line_size: AtomicU32,
122	    /// Free-running count of messages committed: producer
123	    /// resume state, not read by the consumer.
124	    producer_idx: CacheAligned<AtomicU32>,
125	    /// Free-running count of messages released: consumer
126	    /// resume state, not read by the producer.
127	    consumer_idx: CacheAligned<AtomicU32>,
128	    /// App-owned scratch line ([`USER_WORDS`] words): zeroed by
129	    /// init, then never touched by the crate.
130	    user: CacheAligned<[AtomicU32; USER_WORDS]>,
131	}
132	
133	const _: () = assert!(size_of::<Header>() == 4 * CACHE_LINE_SIZE);
134	
135	/// A validated view over a v2 ring region, split into the two
136	/// endpoint handles with [`Ring::split`].
137	///
138	/// - Geometry is snapshotted out of the header at init/attach,
139	///   as the other rings do.
140	/// - Region layout: [`Header`], then M slots of N bytes, each
141	///   opening with its [`SlotHeader`].
142	pub struct Ring<'a> {
143	    /// The region's control block.
144	    header: &'a Header,
145	    /// Base of the slot array.
146	    slots: *mut u8,
147	    /// Snapshot of `header.slot_size`.
148	    slot_size: u32,
149	    /// Snapshot of `header.capacity`.
150	    capacity: u32,
151	    /// Slot-position mask (`capacity - 1`).
152	    mask: u32,
153	    _region: PhantomData<&'a [u8]>,
154	}
155	
156	impl<'a> Ring<'a> {
157	    /// Initialize a fresh region and return the ring over it.
158	    ///
159	    /// - `slot_size`: N bytes per slot, a [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]
160	    ///   multiple, of which [`SLOT_HEADER_BYTES`] are the
161	    ///   crate's.
162	    /// - `capacity`: M slots, a power of two `<= 2^30`, 1
163	    ///   included.
164	    /// - The region must be [`CACHE_LINE_SIZE`]-aligned and at
165	    ///   least [`region_size`] bytes.
166	    pub fn init(region: &'a mut [u8], slot_size: u32, capacity: u32) -> Result<Self, Error> {
167	        validate_geometry(slot_size, capacity)?;
168	        let len = region.len();
169	        // Taken exactly once, as v0 does: a second
170	        // `as_mut_ptr()` would retag the slice and invalidate
171	        // `header` under Stacked Borrows.
172	        let base = region.as_mut_ptr();
173	        let header = header_ptr(base, len)?;
174	        if (len as u64) < region_size(slot_size, capacity) {
175	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
176	        }
177	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the Header checked by header_ptr, region
178	        // is exclusively borrowed for 'a, and any byte pattern is a valid Header
179	        // (all-atomic fields, plain-byte padding).
180	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
181	        header
182	            .layout_version
183	            .store(LAYOUT_VERSION, Ordering::Relaxed);
184	        header.slot_size.store(slot_size, Ordering::Relaxed);
185	        header.capacity.store(capacity, Ordering::Relaxed);
186	        header
187	            .cache_line_size
188	            .store(CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32, Ordering::Relaxed);
189	        header.producer_idx.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);
190	        header.consumer_idx.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);
191	        for word in header.user.iter() {
192	            word.store(0, Ordering::Relaxed);
193	        }
194	        // SAFETY: in bounds, region.len() >= region_size.
195	        let slots = unsafe { base.add(size_of::<Header>()) };
196	        // `seq[i] = i`: every slot claimable for lap 0, and the
197	        // reserved bytes zeroed.
198	        for i in 0..capacity {
199	            // SAFETY: i < capacity, inside the slot array, and
200	            // the slot header's bytes are ours to write before
201	            // the ring is published.
202	            unsafe {
203	                let slot = slots.add(i as usize * slot_size as usize);
204	                core::ptr::write_bytes(slot, 0, SLOT_HEADER_BYTES);
205	                (*(slot as *const SlotHeader))
206	                    .seq
207	                    .store(seq_of(i), Ordering::Relaxed);
208	            }
209	        }
210	        // Published last: a peer that pre-mapped the region must
211	        // never observe MAGIC before the geometry and seqs it
212	        // relies on.
213	        header.magic.store(MAGIC, Ordering::Release);
214	        Ok(Ring {
215	            header,
216	            slots,
217	            slot_size,
218	            capacity,
219	            mask: capacity - 1,
220	            _region: PhantomData,
221	        })
222	    }
223	
224	    /// Attach to a region another process (or an earlier call)
225	    /// already initialized, validating its header.
226	    ///
227	    /// # Safety
228	    ///
229	    /// - `region` points to `len` bytes of memory that outlive
230	    ///   `'a`, genuinely shared and writable (e.g. a
231	    ///   `MAP_SHARED` mapping).
232	    /// - No other producer attaches if this side will produce.
233	    ///   Likewise for the consumer side (SPSC contract).
234	    pub unsafe fn attach(region: *mut u8, len: usize) -> Result<Self, Error> {
235	        let header = header_ptr(region, len)?;
236	        // SAFETY: alignment + room for the Header checked by
237	        // header_ptr. Caller guarantees the memory is live and
238	        // shared.
239	        let header = unsafe { &*header };
240	        // Acquire pairs with init's Release store of magic.
241	        if header.magic.load(Ordering::Acquire) != MAGIC {
242	            return Err(Error::BadMagic);
243	        }
244	        if header.layout_version.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != LAYOUT_VERSION {
245	            return Err(Error::BadLayoutVersion);
246	        }
247	        if header.cache_line_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed) != CACHE_LINE_SIZE as u32 {
248	            return Err(Error::BadCacheLine);
249	        }
250	        // Snapshot geometry once. Per-op paths never re-read it.
251	        let slot_size = header.slot_size.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
252	        let capacity = header.capacity.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
253	        validate_geometry(slot_size, capacity)?;
254	        if (len as u64) < region_size(slot_size, capacity) {
255	            return Err(Error::TooSmall);
256	        }
257	        // SAFETY: in bounds, len >= region_size.
258	        let slots = unsafe { region.add(size_of::<Header>()) };
259	        Ok(Ring {
260	            header,
261	            slots,
262	            slot_size,
263	            capacity,
264	            mask: capacity - 1,
265	            _region: PhantomData,
266	        })
267	    }
268	
269	    /// Split into the producer and consumer endpoint handles.
270	    ///
271	    /// - Consuming `self` makes each handle exist at most once
272	    ///   per ring per process. Cross-process, one producing and
273	    ///   one consuming process is the SPSC contract.
274	    pub fn split(self) -> (Producer<'a>, Consumer<'a>) {
275	        (
276	            Producer::new(
277	                self.header,
278	                self.slots,
279	                self.slot_size,
280	                self.capacity,
281	                self.mask,
282	            ),
283	            Consumer::new(
284	                self.header,
285	                self.slots,
286	                self.slot_size,
287	                self.capacity,
288	                self.mask,
289	            ),
290	        )
291	    }
292	}
293	
294	/// Validate a region base pointer and cast it to the `Header`
295	/// it must start with, shared by [`Ring::init`] /
296	/// [`Ring::attach`].
297	fn header_ptr(base: *mut u8, len: usize) -> Result<*const Header, Error> {
298	    if !(base as usize).is_multiple_of(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) {
299	        return Err(Error::Misaligned);
300	    }
301	    if len < size_of::<Header>() {
302	        return Err(Error::TooSmall);
303	    }
304	    Ok(base as *const Header)
305	}
306	
307	/// Bytes needed for a v2 region with the given geometry: the
308	/// header, then the slots.
309	///
310	/// - Public, as v1's, so a pool that hands out ring segments
311	///   can size its buffers by it.
312	/// - Computed in u64 for the same 32-bit wrap reason as v0's.
313	pub fn region_size(slot_size: u32, capacity: u32) -> u64 {
314	    size_of::<Header>() as u64 + slot_size as u64 * capacity as u64
315	}
316	
317	/// Geometry checks for [`Ring::init`] / [`Ring::attach`].
318	///
319	/// - Slot size as v0, and a line-multiple slot always has room
320	///   for the slot header. Capacity a power of two up to
321	///   [`MAX_CAPACITY`], 1 allowed.
322	fn validate_geometry(slot_size: u32, capacity: u32) -> Result<(), Error> {
323	    if slot_size == 0 || !(slot_size as usize).is_multiple_of(CACHE_LINE_SIZE) {
324	        return Err(Error::BadSlotSize);
325	    }
326	    if capacity == 0 || !capacity.is_power_of_two() || capacity > MAX_CAPACITY {
327	        return Err(Error::BadCapacity);
328	    }
329	    Ok(())
330	}

I've read v2 in full. Before writing about 500 lines of v3, here's the design sketch, including what the code forced, so you can agree it or change it first.

## v3 as it would be built

```rust
// spsc::v3
pub struct Ring<'a>;      // init + split, like v0–v2
pub struct Producer<'a>;  // holds the Pool (sole allocator) + a v2 Producer over its segment
pub struct Consumer<'a>;  // holds a PoolResolver + a v2 Consumer over its segment
pub use crate::spsc::v2::{ReadSlot, WriteSlot};   // hot path is v2's

impl<'a> Ring<'a> {
    pub fn init(pool: Pool<'a>, slot_size: u32, seg_capacity: u32) -> Result<Self, Error>;
    pub fn split(self) -> (Producer<'a>, Consumer<'a>);
}
pub fn segment_size(slot_size: u32, seg_capacity: u32) -> u64; // what the app's pool buffers must hold
```

- **`init`:** takes the application's `Pool` and checks that its `buf_size` holds `segment_size`. It allocates the first segment with `alloc_bytes`, lays a v2 ring over it, and sets the link to "none".
- **`Producer::reserve_slot_with(on_full)`:**
  1. Try the current segment once.
  2. On `Full`, allocate a segment and init a v2 ring in it.
  3. Store "none" in the new segment's link, then store the new segment's index in the old segment's link.
  4. Switch to the new segment.
  - If the pool is exhausted, the wait policy runs.
- **`Consumer::reserve_slot_with(on_empty)`:**
  1. Try once.
  2. On `Empty`, load the link.
     - **Link is "none":** the wait policy runs.
     - **Link is set:** do the second look.
  3. If the second look is still `Empty`, attach to the new segment, then free the old one.
  - A link index outside the pool reads as `Empty`, which matches the crate's rule that corruption fails safe.
- **The link:** `user[0]` in each segment's v2 header. The consequence is that v3's endpoints have no `user()` line of their own.

## What the code forced, beyond what we agreed

1. **Two small crate-private pool helpers, for Rust's aliasing rules.** The producer lays its v2 ring over the buffer, and the consumer attaches to the same buffer from another thread.
   - **The problem:** if the producer's long-lived ring came from the `&mut [u8]` that `DerefMut` hands out, the consumer's first write to that buffer would invalidate the producer's pointers. That's undefined behavior, and Miri would catch it.
   - **The fix:** both sides derive their ring pointers from the pool's own raw buffer pointer. v2 `init` still runs over `&mut seg`, but that ring is dropped straight away. Both sides then use v2 `attach` with the raw pointer.
   - **What it needs:**
     - A crate-private `BufSlot::as_mut_ptr()` that returns the guard's raw pointer.
     - `PoolResolver::slot_from_idx`, which is already crate-private, relaxed to accept `T: ?Sized` so the consumer can get a `[u8]` guard from an index.
   - **Visibility:** neither is public, so the pool's API stays as agreed.
2. **One `unsafe` reborrow in each endpoint's retry loop.** Rust's borrow checker rejects "return the guard borrowed from the current segment, otherwise change segments and loop", a known limitation of today's checker. The workaround is a raw reborrow of the inner v2 endpoint, with a `SAFETY` comment. The returned guard borrows `&mut self` in any case.
3. **An empty pool at `init`.** `Error` has no variant for that. I'd add `Error::Exhausted`, which is a public API addition, fine under 0.16.0.
4. **`Header` at the crate root.** The default re-export includes `Header`, and v3 has no header of its own.

content.text:
Noted: the helpers stay crate-private.

**Why a v2 ring inside each segment.** That came from the draft, and the reason was measurement:
- **Reuse:** v3 reuses v2's claim, commit, and release, which are already tested, and the in-segment hot path is v2's own code.
- **Measurement:** the sweep then compares v3 at `M = depth` against v2 and attributes any difference to the seams alone. That's the prediction on record.

The price of that choice is that every segment carries a whole v2 region:
- **Header:** a four-line v2 header, holding geometry, the producer index, the consumer index, and the user line. Only one word of it (`user[0]`, the link) means anything to v3.
  - **Geometry:** the same in every segment.
  - **The two indices:** restart at 0 in each new segment, and they're resume state v3 never uses without attach.
  - **Seam cost:** every seam writes those four lines and the seqs.
- **At `M = 1`:** a 64-byte message occupies a five-line buffer, and a large part of each seam's cost is writing a header v3 mostly ignores.
- **The indirection:** it forces the v2 `init`-then-`attach` step and the raw-pointer handling I described.

**The alternative: a native v3 segment.** v3 would own its layout:
- **Segment header:** one line, holding the link word and room for a later field.
- **Slots:** the in-slot seq, as in v2, since that's the lesson v2 taught.
- **Geometry:** held once, in the endpoints.
- **Positions:** each endpoint's position inside its segment kept privately in the endpoint, not in shared memory.
- **Payoff:** a seam writes one line plus the slot seqs. An `M = 1` message needs a two-line buffer instead of five. No v2 `init`/`attach` indirection, and the endpoints hold their pointers directly.
- **Costs:** v3 has its own claim, commit, and release, written in v2's style (roughly 150 lines copied and adapted, plus tests). The sweep then compares v3 against v2 as two separate implementations rather than "v2 plus seams".

**How that settles the `Header` question:**
- **With v2 segments:** re-export `v2::Header`, since that is what sits in a segment.
- **With native segments:** v3 has a one-line `SegmentHeader` and nothing resembling `Header`, so the name leaves the crate root, and users name `spsc::v2::Header` explicitly.

My lean is the native segment. v3 is meant to be a real queue layer and the future default, and paying a four-line header per segment, mostly for fields v3 never reads, works against small `M`. The measurement question survives: v3 at `M = depth` against v2 still shows whether the native layout matches v2's hot path.

What would you like to clarify, or do you prefer one of the two?

message.content: A miss-interpretation on v2 -> v3. First v2 remains unchanged so we can benchmark v3 vs v2 vs v1 vs v0. Second, v3 can use anything in v2 where convienent but no requirements one way or the other. I lean towards using indexes over pointers where possible. For instance pool's are defined by indexes, at least that's what I thought.

content.text:
Thanks, that clears it up. v2 stays exactly as it is, so the v0/v1/v2/v3 comparison is clean. v3 can borrow from v2 where that's handy, but doesn't have to.

**Indexes.** Yes, the pool works that way:
- **Free-stack links:** a free buffer's first word holds the next free buffer's index.
- **Head:** `first_free_idx` is an index.
- **Descriptors:** `Desc { pool_id, buf_idx }` carries indexes.
- **Pointers:** computed only at the moment of access, as `bufs + idx * buf_size`, inside the pool.

v3 can follow the same approach:
- **The link:** a buffer index, "none" being `u32::MAX`, as the pool uses.
- **Positions:** each endpoint keeps its slot index inside the segment privately.
- **Pointers:** derived from the pool's base plus the index, recomputed only when an endpoint changes segments. That also dissolves the aliasing problem from my last message. Both sides take their pointers from the one pool base, so v3 never lays a v2 ring over the buffer and never needs `init`-then-`attach`.

That makes v3 a native segment:
- **A small segment header:** one line, holding the link.
- **Then slots:** each carries its own "committed" marker at the front, the lesson v2 taught.

**One real choice: what a segment is.**
- **Circular, the draft's shape:** a segment is a ring. The producer reuses its slots, lap after lap, as the consumer releases them, and only links a new segment when the current one is `Full`.
  - **When seams happen:** only on overflow. When the consumer keeps up, v3 behaves like one ring and never touches the pool.
  - **Protocol:** the consumer needs the second look, because an `Empty` can go stale before it sees the link. Slots need v2-style seq values that distinguish claimable, committed, and released, and each seam initializes them.
- **Linear, a classic segmented queue:** the producer fills slots `0..M` once, then always moves to a new segment. The consumer reads `0..M`, follows the link, and frees the old segment.
  - **When seams happen:** every `M` messages, even when the consumer keeps up. So there's constant pool churn, and that churn is exactly what the sweep would measure.
  - **Protocol:** simpler. A slot is only ever written once per use of the buffer, so it needs just a committed marker, cleared at each seam. The consumer knows a segment is finished when it has read all `M` slots, with no `Empty` race and no second look. The producer is `Full` only when the pool is exhausted.

**My lean is circular.** It matches the Todo's intent: Full stops failing the send, and the queue grows only when it has to, so a queue that keeps up costs what v2 costs. Linear is simpler and easier to prove correct, but it pays a seam every `M` messages forever, which works against using v3 as the default queue.

Which fits what you have in mind, circular or linear? Or should we talk through either one first?

content.text:
A segment is its own ring, and every segment in a queue works the same way. That's the circular shape, and it makes measuring the switch simple.

**The measurement.** At segment depth 1, each segment holds one message. Whenever the producer's next send finds that slot not yet released, it switches to a new segment. The sweep compares v3 at depth 1 against v3 at larger depths, and against v2, and the difference is the switch cost.

One thing to know when reading those numbers: at depth 1 a switch happens only when the producer gets ahead of the consumer. If the consumer releases the slot first, the producer reuses the same segment. So the depth 1 numbers measure switch cost under a producer that runs ahead, which is `tp-stream`'s shape.

**The design as I now understand it:**
- **Segment:** one pool buffer, holding a ring.
  - **Header:** one line, with the link: the next segment's buffer index, or `u32::MAX` for "none".
  - **Slots:** each opens with its seq word, v2's in-slot protocol: claimable at `pos`, committed at `pos + M + 1`, released at `pos + M`. Each segment initializes those seqs once, when it's allocated.
- **Indexes everywhere:** the link and each endpoint's current segment are buffer indexes, and each endpoint's position in its segment is a private index. Pointers come from the pool base plus an index, recomputed only on a switch, so producer and consumer share one pointer origin.
- **Producer:** try the current segment once. On `Full`: allocate a buffer, init its header and seqs, set its link to "none", store its index in the old segment's link, and switch. An exhausted pool is `Full`, and the wait policy runs.
- **Consumer:** try once. On `Empty`: load the link. "None" means wait. Set means the second look: if the old segment is still `Empty`, switch and free the old segment.
- **Relationship to v2:** v2 is untouched. v3 copies the few small helpers it needs, such as the seq arithmetic.
- **Pool:** crate-private helpers only (a raw pointer for a guard, and `slot_from_idx` accepting `[u8]`), no public change.

**Three small decisions left:**
1. **`Header` at the crate root:** v3's segment header isn't a ring header, so I'd drop `Header` from the default re-export. Users who want v2's name it `spsc::v2::Header`.
2. **Empty pool at `init`:** add `Error::Exhausted`.
3. **Lending the producer's pool:** leave it out for now.

Do those three work for you, and does the design above match what you mean?

content.text:
That's a better fit for what the queue is meant to be, and it changes where the cost lands.

**Where the cost goes:**
- **At `init`:** the ring takes all of its segments from the pool, say `seg_count` of them, and initializes their headers and seqs once.
- **During operation:** no pool alloc or free, and no segment initialization. A switch is only "move to a segment that's already set up".
- **The measurement:** at depth 1 it measures that switch and nothing else.

**What a switch needs, then.** Drained segments have to get back to the producer:
- **Pool free-stack, reused privately:** the consumer frees a drained segment into a set only this ring uses, and the producer pops from it. It works, but it's a CAS on a head word both sides write, so a cache line crosses cores on every switch.
- **A return path that uses only plain loads and stores:** since there is exactly one consumer and one producer, the consumer can hand segment indexes back through a small SPSC index ring sized `seg_count`, and the producer takes them from there. v3 would then stay CAS-free, like v0 through v2. That matters for the no-CAS embedded targets the design note keeps in view.

**Reuse without re-initializing.** A fully drained segment is left in a consistent state: every slot's seq is at its "released" value, and the producer's and consumer's positions in that segment are equal.
- **The idea:** if the segment's header records that shared position when it's handed back, the producer can pick the segment up and continue its laps from there, with no seq initialization at all.
- **What a switch costs then:** a link store, a hand-back, and reading one header line. That's about as close to "only switching" as it gets.

**What changes compared to taking segments from the pool as needed:**
- **Capacity is fixed:** `seg_capacity × seg_count`, and `Full` means "no free segment" rather than "pool exhausted". It's still elastic in the sense that the chain grows and shrinks among its own segments, and a queue that keeps up stays in one hot segment.
- **Memory is reserved:** a quiet queue still holds `seg_count` buffers. With many queues that each burst rarely, a shared pool would use less memory. We could note that tradeoff in the design note, and pick per-ring sets for speed.
- **`init`'s signature** gains `seg_count` again, close to the original draft. The segments still come from the application's pool, just all at once.
- **The "return the last segment" Todo** mostly stops mattering, because the segments belong to the ring for its whole life. I'd drop it.

The plain version: take all of a ring's segments at startup, so running the queue never allocates. Drained segments go back to the producer through a simple no-CAS return path, and a segment can be reused as it was left, without resetting it. Then the only runtime cost is switching, which depth 1 measures, and the price is a fixed capacity and memory reserved even while the queue is idle.

content.text:
That goal makes the design much sharper. The overflow segments are insurance: they cost nothing unless the producer outruns the consumer.

**What "never any cost" requires of the fast path:**
- **Producer:** while its segment isn't `Full`, it touches only that segment's slot lines, exactly like v2. The link, the return path, and the other segments are touched only on `Full`, which is the case where the insurance pays out.
- **Consumer:** a consumer faster than the producer spends a lot of time finding its segment `Empty`, and on `Empty` it has to check the link. That's one read of the segment's header line on each empty poll.
  - **Why it's cheap:** in steady state the producer never writes that line, since it only writes the link on a switch. So the line stays in the consumer's own cache, and no line bounces between cores.
  - **Tuning, if the sweep shows it:** it's an extra load per empty poll on the wait path, not per message. If it ever mattered, the consumer could check the link less often, for example every few empty polls, since correctness only needs it to check eventually.
- **Allocation:** none, since segments are set up at `init`. Hand-backs use plain stores, not CAS.

**How overflow plays out.** Say the producer bursts and fills segment A. It switches to B, and maybe C. The consumer drains A, follows the link to B, and hands A back. Once the burst ends, the consumer catches up, and both sides settle into whichever segment is current, with the other segments idle in the return path. "The first segment" isn't a fixed one; what matters is that in steady state only one segment is in use.

**One risk: thrashing at the boundary.** If the producer runs just slightly faster than the consumer for a long time, it may switch often, and each switch pays the link and hand-back cost. That's the "unexpected worst case" costing something, which is expected. The sweep at depth 1 would show the upper bound on it.

**What this does to the acceptance check.** The key test becomes: v3 with the consumer keeping up matches v2 at the same segment depth, within run noise. That's the "no cost" claim. Depth 1 with a producer that runs ahead measures the switch cost. Both fit into `tp-stream` and `tp-matrix`: the round trip keeps the consumer ahead, and the stream lets the producer run ahead.

The plain version: when the consumer keeps up, v3 should cost exactly what v2 costs, touching only its current segment. The extra segments only come into play when the producer gets ahead, and that's the only time switching costs anything. The benchmarks should show both of those.

With the design settled, I'll update the cycle record to match: segments prepared at `init`, a CAS-free return path, reuse without re-initializing, and the reframed acceptance check. I'll also bring the three open decisions (`Header` at the root, `Error::Exhausted`, not lending the pool) for a yes or no before writing code. Should I go ahead with that?
